entries.claim: On its Q1 FY2026 call (23 Jul 2026) Albertsons reaffirmed AI as "foundational" and guided FY26 capex of $1.9-2.0bn toward store modernization and AI capabilities, but disclosed no AI-attributed revenue metric. The 10% Ask AI basket-size lift CEO Susan Morris put on the record on the 7 Jan 2026 call was not repeated. Digital sales grew 13%, not attributed to AI.
entries.source_name: Q1 FY2026 earnings call, complete transcript (prior claim: Q3 FY2025 call, 7 Jan 2026, via PYMNTS / CX Today)
entries.mechanism: Ask AI conversational search in the Albertsons/Safeway/Vons/Jewel-Osco mobile apps surfaces complementary items mid-search, expanding the basket; household-level personalized offers on top of ~tens of millions of loyalty households. The mechanism is real and the January number was specific; what is missing is any repeat measurement.
entries.shape_justification: S2, and counter-evidence to it. Basket expansion inside an existing customer base buying existing groceries in existing stores - absent the AI, these shoppers buy groceries from somebody. Zero-sum at industry level, GDP-neutral. Logged as counter-evidence because the only quantified revenue-side AI metric this company had ever disclosed vanished from the next disclosure while AI capex was reaffirmed and expanded. Four named enterprise AI priorities were given (digital CX, merchandising intelligence, labor optimization, supply chain optimization); three of the four are cost-side, and the revenue-side one carried no number.
entries.falsifier: Reverse-falsifier: if Albertsons re-discloses the Ask AI basket-size lift, or any successor revenue-attributed AI metric at or above 10%, on the Q2 FY2026 call (expected Oct 2026), this entry is a reporting artifact and should be downgraded. If two more quarters pass with AI capex reaffirmed and still no AI-attributed revenue number, treat the January figure as a one-off marketing disclosure rather than a managed KPI.
entries.confidence_why: Absence-of-evidence is weaker than a stated walk-back; the July transcript was read via a summarizing fetch, so a passing mention could have been missed. The January 10% figure is Tier C reporting (two independent outlets) of a Tier A call, not the transcript itself.

entries.company: S&P 500 (510 firms, 2016-2025) - MIT FutureTech / CMU study
entries.claim: Peer-style study of AI adoption in 510 S&P 500 firms, scored from SEC 10-K language: in 2025 only 11% had AI "deeply integrated into their business processes", plus a further 10% "using AI in the production of goods and delivery of services", up from 5% in 2022. The technology sector "accounts for two-thirds of deeply integrated enterprise adoption", with only "slowly accelerating adoption among non-technology firms". Profitability follows a J-curve from no adoption to deep adoption, but the authors "observe no differences in capex or productivity".
entries.source_name: Yu, Fleming, Hampton, Combemale & Thompson, "AI Adoption in S&P 500 Firms", arXiv 2607.08920 (submitted 9 Jul 2026)
entries.mechanism: Not a deployment finding - a measurement of the population this log samples from. Adoption is scored off 10-K language, which sits under liability for materially false statements, so it is a harder measure than survey self-report. The finding that matters here is the denominator: two-thirds of genuinely deep enterprise AI adoption sits inside the technology sector, i.e. inside the population METHOD excludes as subjects.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence, tagged to S2 because S2 is where the bulk of revenue-attribution claims live, but it cuts against S3 equally. A J-curve in profitability with no measured productivity or capex difference is a margin story, not a top-line story; the paper finds no top-line effect to report. Directly bears on why this log's positive column is empty: the non-tech incumbents it tracks are precisely the slow-adopting tail, so scarce revenue disclosure may reflect thin real adoption rather than adoption without payoff. Those are very different worlds and this study does not separate them.
entries.falsifier: If a later vintage of this measure (2026-27 10-Ks) shows non-tech deep adoption converging toward tech-sector levels while revenue-side disclosure stays absent, the 'thin adoption' explanation dies and 'adoption without top-line payoff' is the live one. If non-tech deep adoption stays under ~10% of firms, this log should expect a structurally empty positive column and should not read that as evidence AI does not produce revenue.
entries.confidence_why: Primary abstract retrieved and quoted directly; paper body not read this run. Preprint, not yet peer reviewed. Secondary coverage (theaiinsider.tech, 14 Jul) additionally claims the study found 'little evidence that AI adoption was associated with higher revenue per employee' - that line is NOT in the abstract and is unverified against the paper body, so it is excluded from the claim above. Source is 17 days old, outside the trailing-48h window, logged as a strong prior-fortnight item.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (23 Jul 2026) CEO Vimal Kapur guided software ARR growth of ~15% for 2026 and said the business will "inch from about $900 million to a little over $1 billion of ARR in that segment this year." He described Forge as "the primary mechanism for delivering 'physical AI' to customers" and named software ARR as "the best way to measure our progress" toward autonomy. No revenue was attributed to AI itself.
entries.source_name: Honeywell Q2 2026 earnings call transcript (Motley Fool); 15% ARR figure corroborated in Investing.com transcript
entries.mechanism: Honeywell Forge is the connected-plant software layer sold on top of Honeywell's installed automation base (Kapur: "we have been selling automation since 1975"). It is sold as subscription ARR, and the AI/autonomy content is being positioned as the reason customers move up the subscription tiers. The revenue mechanism is software attach onto existing hardware relationships, not a new product with no predecessor.
entries.shape_justification: S2. Test: absent this AI capability, would the buyer have bought something similar from somebody? Yes - industrial asset-performance and process-optimization software is a contested category (AVEVA, Siemens, GE Vernova, ABB, Rockwell). Growth here is share taken inside an existing budget line, zero-sum at industry level and GDP-neutral. Explicitly NOT S3: Forge has a predecessor in Honeywell's own catalog going back years, and no capability gate at the 24-month frontier is established. The attribution weakness is the point of logging it: this is the largest AI-linked top-line number a non-tech industrial put on the record this quarter, and management still did not attribute a single dollar of it to AI - only to "Forge offerings" and "the launch of new software products." 'Physical AI' is the framing wrapped around a pre-existing software line.
entries.falsifier: Forge/segment software ARR failing to print above $1.0bn on the Q4 2026 / FY26 results, or the ~15% ARR growth rate not being restated on the Q3 2026 call. Second and sharper falsifier: if Honeywell never breaks out an AI-attributed revenue figure across FY26-FY27 while continuing to describe Forge as its physical-AI delivery mechanism, treat the AI framing as a repositioning of existing software revenue rather than an AI result.
entries.confidence_why: The 15% ARR growth guide is corroborated across two independent transcripts. The $900m-to-$1bn absolute figure was verified verbatim by direct retrieval but appears in only one transcript source, and Kapur's phrase "that segment" is not unambiguously tied to a named reporting segment in the retrieved text - do not treat the $900m base as an audited segment disclosure. Status is PROJECTED because it is a within-year guide, not a realized print.

entries.company: Grant Thornton 2026 AI Impact Survey - manufacturing cut (n=100 of 950)
entries.claim: Survey of 950 business leaders across 10 industries, fielded 23 Feb - 18 Mar 2026: "Among manufacturing respondents, zero reported significant revenue uplift from AI initiatives, compared to 12% of executives across all industries. Zero reported significant cost savings, again compared to 12% overall." 47% of manufacturers reported only minimal revenue uplift; 64% reported increased efficiency. Manufacturers led all sectors in operational AI deployment (62%) while reporting the weakest financial return.
entries.source_name: Grant Thornton, "Manufacturing insights: 2026 AI Impact Survey Report" (survey fielded 23 Feb - 18 Mar 2026; press coverage 9 Jul 2026)
entries.mechanism: Not a deployment finding - a base-rate measurement of the population this log samples from, and the cleanest available quantification of the efficiency-without-revenue gap: 64% report efficiency gains, 0% report significant revenue uplift, in the sector with the HIGHEST operational deployment rate. If efficiency mechanically converted to top line, the sector leading deployment should not be the sector reporting zero.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence, tagged to S2 because S2 (attributed incremental revenue on existing products) is the shape most non-tech corporates claim and the shape this null result most directly contradicts. It also constrains S3 by implication: a sector reporting zero significant revenue uplift is not opening new markets. The 58%-vs-15% headline elsewhere in the same survey (fully-integrated vs piloting firms reporting AI-driven revenue growth) is a selection-effect artifact, not causal evidence - firms that integrate deeply are firms that already saw something work - and should not be cited as offsetting the manufacturing zero.
entries.falsifier: The 2027 wave of the same survey showing manufacturing significant-revenue-uplift materially above zero, or a Q3/Q4 2026 cluster of named manufacturers disclosing AI-attributed revenue. Either would mean this reading was a timing artifact of a sector mid-J-curve rather than a structural absence.
entries.confidence_why: Tier D, and METHOD says Tier D is never the sole basis for an entry. Logged anyway with that conflict stated, on one specific ground: the systematic-inflation bias that justifies distrusting Tier D runs the OTHER WAY here - Grant Thornton sells AI advisory and is publishing a zero against its own commercial interest. Remaining limits are real: self-reported, non-random sample, "significant" undefined by the respondent, n=100 subgroup, and the field window (Feb-Mar 2026) is ~5 months stale relative to today. Age also exceeds the 14-day window; included because it is unlogged and directly load-bearing on the thesis.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (22 Jul 2026) CEO Trevor Burgess said the newly live quote-to-bind model is "definitely having a positive impact on the new business sales"; ~3,700 agents exchanged 33,000 messages with the Atlas+ assistant during the quarter. Q2 revenue $55.9m (+33% YoY), written premium $126.9m (+31%), lifetime written loss ratio 19.5%, FY26 revenue guided to $199m. None of the revenue is attributed to either system.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (22 Jul); figures corroborated by the 21 Jul results release
entries.mechanism: Two distinct systems in the revenue path. (1) A machine-learning quote-to-bind model inside Triton, the underwriting platform, scoring and routing submissions with no human underwriter in the loop. (2) Atlas+, an agent-facing assistant sitting on the quote screen answering the writing agent's questions in real time and drafting follow-up email, with a ranked next-best-task feed due in Q3. The stated route to revenue is higher agent quoting throughput and a better quote-to-bind conversion rate.
entries.shape_justification: S1, not S2 or S3. Every disclosed number is an input metric - agent count, message count - and the revenue statement is qualitative. Management gave a precise written-premium figure ($126.9m) and a precise FY guide ($199m) and attributed neither to the AI: this is the S1 conversion silence in its purest form, from a company that is otherwise unusually forthcoming. The S3 read was run and failed: >55% of new business outside mandatory flood zones and >75% voluntary purchase looks like new demand, but NFIP already writes voluntary policies outside the SFHA, so test (b) fails on prior alternative; and Burgess said flatly "We're not using AI to set pricing... All of the AI that we're using is algorithmic," which fails test (c) on the capability gate. Appendix, not main, because the subject is out of scope in its own words - the 21 Jul release calls Neptune an "AI-native managing general agent" that "operates without human underwriters." It does not test whether an ordinary incumbent gets revenue ROI from AI spend; it tests whether an AI-native entrant can take share in a boring line. Logged so that comparator stays visible rather than being discarded.
entries.falsifier: By the Q4 2026 / FY26 call, a disclosed quote-to-bind conversion delta or bound-premium dollar figure attributable to the model. If Atlas+ engagement counts keep growing across Q3 and Q4 while the conversion number never appears, the quote-to-bind claim was narrative and the 31-33% growth was distribution and pricing, not AI.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call, named executive, on-the-record quotes, and hard quarter figures from the results release - but zero of the revenue is AI-attributed, and an AI-native subject cannot test the incumbent thesis this log exists to test.

entries.claim: In the Q1 FY27 results release (23 Jul 2026) Infosys disclosed "AI as a % of Revenue" of 8.2% on total revenue of $5,082m (derived: approx. $417m), up from approximately 5.5% two quarters earlier. CEO Salil Parekh: "AI momentum is now rapidly converting into revenue, which demonstrates how Infosys' differentiated enterprise AI value proposition is translating into consistent market share gains." In the same release Infosys narrowed FY27 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to 1.5%-3.0% from 1.5%-3.5%, with reported growth of 2.4% YoY in constant currency.
entries.source_name: Infosys Q1 FY27 results release / Form 6-K, 23 Jul 2026; definition of the metric and the deflation commentary from Dataquest deep dive of the same call (Tier C, secondary)
entries.mechanism: Infosys sells AI-first services across six named value pools - AI strategy, process redesign, agents, data modernisation, AI engineering, platform-led implementation. Per Dataquest's account of the call, the metric deliberately EXCLUDES conventional engagements that merely have AI tools bolted onto existing workflows; those are tracked internally and not disclosed. That is a materially tighter definition than the 'AI-influenced revenue' constructs METHOD rejects, and it is the reason this is loggable at all. Running the other way, management described client pressure to use coding assistants and agents to complete existing work with fewer people and hours - reported as 'AI-led deflation' - compressing application maintenance, infrastructure operations and software development revenue, and said the two effects 'cannot always be separated cleanly' because clients bundle productivity concessions into contracts that also award new AI work.
entries.shape_justification: S2, and the CEO says so himself: 'market share gains'. Absent Infosys' AI capability these buyers would have bought transformation and engineering services from Accenture, TCS, Wipro, Cognizant or Capgemini - test (a) fails for S3, a competitor lost the sale. Test (c) is arguably passed (agentic delivery is a genuine post-2024 capability) but capability novelty alone does not make new demand. Zero-sum at industry level; GDP-neutral. Subject is out of scope for the main log in METHOD's own terms - an IT services firm selling AI implementation is a shovel vendor, and its AI revenue describes its own sales rather than a corporate's deployment ROI - so it is routed to the appendix and never counted. Flagged counter_evidence because the pairing is the finding: AI revenue share rose roughly 50% in two quarters and the company cut total growth guidance in the same release. Gross AI revenue up, net top line down. This is the sharpest quantification yet found of AI revenue substituting for the base rather than adding to it - and it comes from a firm whose whole business is selling AI, which is the population most incentivised to show the opposite.
entries.falsifier: If AI-first revenue share keeps climbing through FY27 (Q2 and Q3) while constant-currency total growth guidance stays at or below 3%, the substitution read is confirmed and the 8.2% is a mix metric, not a growth metric. Conversely, if total cc growth guidance is raised above 3% while AI share rises, AI revenue is genuinely additive and this entry is wrong. Second falsifier: if Infosys stops publishing 'AI as a % of Revenue' - a disclosure a company retires when the number stops flattering it.
entries.confidence_why: The 8.2%, the revenue base and the guidance are Tier A primary. The six-value-pool definition, the ~5.5% prior-quarter comparator and the 'AI-led deflation' language reach me only through one trade-press deep dive of the call, not the transcript itself - load-bearing and second-hand, so flagged.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (29 Jul 2026) management said the new Architects & Engineers product was "brought to market earlier this month using what we estimate to be approximately 60% fewer resources because of AI," and that the company has "all but eliminated" the fixed cost of launching a new product. Q2 gross written premium was more than $205m, up 22%+, with no premium attributed to AI or broken out for the new lines.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript) + 10 Jul 2026 pre-announcement release
entries.mechanism: Product-launch capacity, not underwriting. Ategrity uses AI (including agentic tooling across marketing and governance) to build and file a new specialty line - forms, rating, appetite, distribution collateral - with roughly 60% of the previous internal resource. The revenue path is that a carrier which previously could only afford to stand up large classes can now stand up smaller ones, so the addressable set of classes widens. The premium consequence is entirely undisclosed.
entries.shape_justification: S1, not S3, and the distinction is the whole point. The disclosed number is an input metric (resources consumed to launch), never revenue. On the S3 tests: (a) counterfactual purchase fails - an architects-and-engineers buyer would have bought A&E cover from one of many existing carriers; (b) prior alternative fails for the same reason, this is an old, competitively written class, so any premium won here is taken from a competitor; (c) capability gate is arguable at best - form drafting and filing support does not obviously require a post-2024 frontier model; (d) newly economic is the only test with any pull, and only for Ategrity's own economics, not for the segment. Revenue conversion was conspicuously NOT disclosed: the 10 Jul pre-announcement says "recently launched products... began contributing meaningfully" and attaches no dollar figure, and the call attributes none of the 22%+ premium growth to AI. Note also that this is the closest any incumbent in this log has come to articulating the METHOD cost-collapse-opens-a-segment mechanism in its own words - "all but eliminated the fixed cost of launching a new product" is the S3 pathway stated without the S3 evidence.
entries.falsifier: If Q3/Q4 2026 or FY26 disclosure never breaks out premium from the classes launched under the low-cost regime - A&E and the other 2026 launches - and the launch-cost claim is not repeated with a revenue figure attached, this was a cost anecdote dressed as a growth story. Specific check: does Ategrity ever name a class it wrote only because the launch cost fell?
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call, named company, management's own estimate corroborated in two independent write-ups of the same call - but it is an ESTIMATED input metric with zero revenue attached, and "60% fewer resources" is unauditable.

entries.claim: In the Q2 2026 results release (22 Jul 2026) ServiceNow disclosed that "ServiceNow AI crossed $1 billion in annual contract value in Q2 2026," against subscription revenue of $3,877m (+24.5% y/y) and cRPO of $13.20bn (+21%), with a stated long-term goal of AI reaching 30% of annual contract value by 2030.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 results release
entries.mechanism: AI SKUs (Now Assist and the agentic workflow products) sold as priced add-ons into an installed base of largely non-tech enterprises, booked as incremental annual contract value on top of the platform subscription.
entries.shape_justification: Appendix: the subject is an enterprise software vendor, so this is the vendor's own sales, not a deploying corporation's ROI - it is a shovel number. Logged anyway for the same reason the Infosys entry was (29 Jul): it is the demand-side mirror of this log's central absence. Somebody is paying $1bn a year for AI, and the buyers are overwhelmingly the non-tech incumbents whose own calls attribute nothing to it. Classified S2 rather than S3-CANDIDATE because ServiceNow does not disclose the incremental-versus-substitution split - whether AI ACV is net-new enterprise budget or a re-bundling of workflow and RPA spend those customers would have committed anyway. The capability gate (c) plausibly passes for agentic production deployments; (a) and (b) are simply not established, and per METHOD an unestablished counterfactual does not get promoted.
entries.falsifier: The $1bn is ACV, not recognised revenue and not customer-measured value. If AI ACV growth decelerates sharply while total subscription growth holds, the number was a reclassification of existing spend. Harder test: the 30%-of-ACV-by-2030 goal implies roughly $9-10bn of AI ACV - watch whether the annual disclosure keeps compounding toward it or the metric quietly disappears from the release, which is the pattern already seen with Albertsons.
entries.confidence_why: Company-issued results release, unambiguous verbatim figure, quoted identically in independent coverage of the same print.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (24 Jul 2026) CEO Stephen Squeri said AI has produced "anywhere from a 30 to 40% decrease in cycle time from a coding perspective" - and immediately disclaimed it as a saving: "Now that's really not a savings because what that does is allows us to do more." No dollar amount, no headcount reduction, no AI-attributed expense figure anywhere on the call.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript)
entries.mechanism: AI coding assistance inside Amex's own technology organisation, compressing the elapsed time from requirement to shipped code. Squeri names technology as "one of the first places that we have deployed it." The gain is explicitly converted into throughput, not into a smaller technology budget.
entries.shape_justification: C3 - non-tech subject, software engineering function. The most useful thing here is the disclaimer. Trap 2 in METHOD: a CEO volunteering that a productivity gain is reinvested rather than banked. CFO Le Caillec guided operating expense to "mid-single digits" for the year and said "AI is going to play a critical role in that" - with no AI-specific figure attached, so the expense guide cannot be credited to AI. Servicing headcount discussed qualitatively only: hiring "really hasn't grown and we would expect over time for that number to decrease." Verified against two independent transcripts; the widely circulated phrasing "AI is already reducing coding cycle times by 30% to 40%" is a paraphrase and is not quoted here.
entries.falsifier: If Amex's technology expense line, or total operating expense growth, never bends below the mid-single-digit trend while the coding-cycle claim keeps being repeated, then 30-40% faster coding is a throughput story with no P&L consequence - exactly as Squeri said it was. Watch whether any later call converts it into a dollar or a headcount.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A transcript, named CEO, figure and disclaimer cross-checked in two independent transcripts.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (15 Jul 2026) CFO Dermot McDonogh said that of "our engineers at BNY, roughly 40% of the software written is now written using AI." CEO Robin Vince declined to quantify any benefit - "We don't break out the very specific economic numbers" - and McDonogh de-attributed the headcount decline: "It's down 7% over the year, but that's as a result of everything."
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript)
entries.mechanism: AI coding tools across BNY's engineering organisation, inside an engineering budget management sizes at "approximately $4 billion" - within which McDonogh describes AI spend as "quite de minimis and quite modest."
entries.shape_justification: C3, and a textbook instance of METHOD trap 1: 40% is an ADOPTION metric, not a cost saving. Nothing follows from it about expense. Vince frames the output as capacity rather than savings - "It would be a mistake to think about this capacity as just an efficiency creator" - and when Mike Mayo asked directly for expense-savings or revenue numbers, Vince answered "it's not that we can't identify benefits, we certainly can. It's that we recognize that all of these things coming together are ultimately the success." The only nearby dollar figures - ~$500mm incremental investment and ~$450mm of 2026 efficiency savings - are firmwide and not AI-attributed. Note the correction to this log's own earlier reading: the 27 Jul day record placed this call on 22 Jul (a publication date) and attributed "capacity creator" to the CFO; it is Vince, in Q&A, on 15 Jul.
entries.falsifier: BNY has now twice declined to quantify. If the ~$450mm efficiency line is delivered and management still will not attribute any share of it to AI, then AI at BNY is a capability programme, not a cost programme, and the 40% is a vanity metric. Conversely a first AI-attributed dollar in any 2027 disclosure would be a genuine update.
entries.confidence_why: Two independent transcripts agree on every quote; the refusal to quantify is explicit and repeated, which makes it hard to misread.

entries.claim: Bank of America's official Q2 2026 presentation materials (call 14 Jul 2026, slide 20) disclose "~19K developers leveraging real-time coding assistance, increasing productivity >20%," alongside ~200K active users generating ">400K prompts per day" and ">300 AI / machine learning use cases approved | 114 live generative AI use cases with 34 fully deployed." No dollar saving and no AI-attributed headcount figure was given.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 presentation materials, slide 20 + earnings call
entries.mechanism: Coding assistance across ~19,000 developers, plus AI embedded in operations, risk, finance and client-facing workflows. Moynihan's framing is capacity, not cost: "the same amount of money in '27 will get us more code for lack of a better term, in '28."
entries.shape_justification: C3. Correction to this log's 26 Jul day record, which attributed ">20% developer productivity" to Moynihan on the call: the figure appears only as a slide-20 bullet in the official presentation materials. Moynihan's spoken version is qualitative - "Our developers code more efficiently." Still Tier A, since the deck is a filed investor document, but the attribution matters. Moynihan does claim economics for the portfolio - "over 300 AI use cases approved - all of which have good economics" - without disclosing any of them. Borthwick's headcount comment is explicitly not AI-attributed: "flat to slightly down" on discipline. FY26 operating leverage guidance of "300 to 400 basis points" is not AI-attributed either.
entries.falsifier: A >20% productivity gain across 19,000 developers is roughly 3,800 developer-equivalents. If technology expense and total headcount stay flat-to-up while that claim persists across quarters, the gain is being spent on more software rather than less cost - which is a legitimate choice, but it is not a cost saving and should stop being read as one.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A document and unambiguous figure, but it is a self-reported productivity percentage with no stated measurement method and no dollar conversion.

entries.claim: On the Q4 2025 call (28 Jan 2026) CFO Susan Li said: "Since the beginning of 2025, we've seen a 30% increase in output per engineer, with the majority of that growth coming from the adoption of agentic coding, which saw a big jump in Q4," and "We're seeing even stronger gains with power users of AI coding tools, whose output has increased 80% year-over-year." No dollar amount and no headcount effect attributed.
entries.source_name: Q4 2025 earnings call, official transcript
entries.mechanism: Agentic coding tools across Meta's engineering organisation, measured as output per engineer rather than as cost. Zuckerberg on the same call: "We're starting to see projects that used to require big teams now be accomplished by a single very talented person."
entries.shape_justification: C1 - the easy cell, and the benchmark against which C3 and C4 should be read. This is the clearest quantified engineering-productivity claim from any large company, on a first-party transcript, and it still contains no dollars and no headcount. Meta's May 2026 workforce reduction was framed by Zuckerberg as funding AI capex, not as harvesting AI productivity, so the two must not be joined into a saving. Output per engineer is Meta's own internal construct; the measurement method is not published.
entries.falsifier: If output per engineer keeps compounding at 30%+ while Meta's engineering headcount and total expense also keep rising, the gain is being reinvested in scope, not converted to cost - the same pattern Amex states openly. A single AI-attributed dollar of expense reduction from Meta would be the update.
entries.confidence_why: First-party official transcript PDF, named CFO, verbatim, unambiguous figures.

entries.claim: CEO Sundar Pichai, at Google Cloud Next (April 2026): "Today, 75% of all new code at Google is now AI-generated and approved by engineers, up from 50% last fall." On the same stage: "a particularly complex code migration done by agents and engineers working together was completed six times faster than was possible a year ago with engineers alone." In his Q2 2026 earnings remarks (22 Jul 2026) he added that "a team in Chrome is now on track to accelerate delivery by eight times, compressing a two-year timeline into three months through model-driven refactoring."
entries.source_name: Google Cloud Next 2026 keynote post (company blog) + Alphabet Q2 2026 CEO remarks
entries.mechanism: AI code generation and agentic refactoring across Google's engineering organisation, with the migration and Chrome examples given as elapsed-time compression on specific projects.
entries.shape_justification: C1. The 75% is a pure ADOPTION metric (METHOD trap 1) and is the single most misquoted number in this field - the wording is 75% of all NEW code, not 75% of Google's code, and Pichai attaches no cost saving, no headcount effect and no dollar to it. The 6x and 8x figures are project-level elapsed-time claims, not a cost line. Logged because the trajectory (50% -> 75% in roughly two quarters) is real information about engineering practice, and because the absence of any cost figure behind the most-cited adoption statistic in the industry is itself the finding.
entries.falsifier: Alphabet has never converted any of these into an expense number. If AI-generated code share saturates near 100% with no disclosed effect on engineering cost, headcount or shipping cadence in the financials, the metric was never about cost. Watch for a first cost or headcount attribution in a 10-K or on a call rather than a keynote.
entries.confidence_why: Tier B company blog, verbatim and on-the-record from the CEO - but a keynote, not a filing, and an adoption metric rather than a result.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2024 call (1 Aug 2024) CEO Andy Jassy said: "With Q's code transformation capabilities, Amazon has migrated over 30,000 Java JDK applications in a few months, saving the company $260 million and 4,500 developer years compared to what it would have otherwise cost." Logged 2026-07-30 as a deliberately dated benchmark: it remains the only dollar-quantified AI engineering saving found from any company, and Amazon's April 2026 shareholder letter contains no comparable figure.
entries.source_name: Q2 2024 earnings call (transcript)
entries.mechanism: Automated Java version-migration across ~30,000 applications, priced as the labour that would otherwise have been required. Explicitly counterfactual - "compared to what it would have otherwise cost" - so it is cost avoidance on work Amazon chose to do, not a reduction in an existing expense line.
entries.shape_justification: C1, and logged with its age stated up front because the age is the point. This figure is two years old, it is the only engineering-function dollar figure anyone has published, and no company has repeated the trick since - including Amazon. That is a strong signal about how hard it is to convert coding productivity into an auditable number: the one clean case was a mechanical, countable migration with an obvious counterfactual, which is exactly the kind of work that does NOT generalise to feature development. METHOD trap 5 applies: this is cost avoidance, not realized reduction.
entries.falsifier: Already partly falsified as a general claim by two years of silence. If no company - Amazon included - publishes a comparable engineering-function dollar figure by end-2026 despite adoption metrics at 40-75%, then coding productivity is structurally unbankable and every C1/C3 percentage should be discounted accordingly.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A transcript, named CEO, explicit counterfactual framing. Confidence is in the quote, not in its currency - the figure is deliberately old and flagged as such.

entries.claim: In an SEC Form 8-K dated 15 Apr 2026, CEO Evan Spiegel told employees Snap would cut "approximately 1,000 team members at Snap, including 16% of our full time employees, in addition to closing more than 300 open roles," and that "we expect to reduce our annualized cost base by more than $500 million by the second half of 2026." The accompanying investor update is headed "AI-Driven Transformation"; adjusted OpEx guidance was cut ~$250m to ~$2.75bn and SBC ~$150m to ~$1.05bn.
entries.source_name: Form 8-K, Exhibits 99.1 and 99.2 (Item 2.05)
entries.mechanism: Workforce reduction concentrated outside engineering, with the stated rationale that "rapid advancements in artificial intelligence enable our teams to reduce repetitive work, increase velocity, and better support our community, partners, and advertisers." The investor update cites a support agent answering "1M+ questions/month" and an AI code-review agent finding "7,500+ bugs."
entries.shape_justification: C2, and the highest-grade source in this ledger - an SEC filing with a quantified Item 2.05 charge ($95-130m pre-tax), not a press release. But METHOD trap 4 applies hard and must not be smoothed: Spiegel attributes the >$500m to "these changes" broadly - prioritisation and restructuring - while the investor deck FRAMES the programme as AI-driven. Snap does not state that AI caused $500m of savings, and this entry must not be read as "AI saved Snap $500m." What Snap did do, uniquely, is put the AI rationale and the dollar number in the same filed document, which is why it is logged. Status PROJECTED: the $500m is estimated on the second half of 2026 and had not been realized at filing.
entries.falsifier: Adjusted OpEx of ~$2.75bn and SBC of ~$1.05bn are hard, checkable numbers. If FY2026 lands at or above the prior ~$3.0bn / ~$1.2bn, the saving did not materialise. Second test: whether headcount stays down through 2027 or quietly rebuilds, which is what happened to the canonical Klarna case.
entries.confidence_why: SEC filing, verbatim, with checkable guidance revisions. The uncertainty is in AI's causal share, not in the numbers - and that uncertainty is stated above rather than papered over.

entries.claim: On the Q1 2026 call (22 Apr 2026) CFO James Kavanaugh said AI-driven internal transformation has "driven $4.5 billion of productivity savings, with an additional $1 billion expected in 2026." On the Q4 2025 call CEO Arvind Krishna described the same figure differently - "exiting 2025 with $4.5 billion of annual run rate savings" rising to "$5.5 billion by the end of next year" - and said "Our entire developer workforce is using Bob with average productivity gains of 45%."
entries.source_name: Q1 2026 earnings call + Q4 2025 earnings call (transcripts)
entries.mechanism: Enterprise-wide AI deployment across HR, customer support, procurement, finance and IT operations. IBM's own function-level detail: $165m of operational savings in customer support since 2022, $600m in enterprise IT since 2022, and 94% of common employee inquiries answered by AskHR without human intervention.
entries.shape_justification: C2 - largest dollar figure in this ledger, and logged with its internal inconsistency exposed rather than resolved. Krishna calls the $4.5bn "annual run rate savings" exiting 2025; Kavanaugh calls it "productivity savings since 2023," i.e. cumulative. These are materially different claims about the same number and IBM has not reconciled them. METHOD trap 3 also applies: "productivity savings" is IBM's own non-GAAP construct, not a GAAP expense line. The 45% Project Bob developer figure is a C1-shaped claim inside the same company; not split into a second entry, per the one-disclosure-one-ledger rule, but noted here because IBM is the only company claiming both an engineering percentage and an enterprise dollar.
entries.falsifier: The reconciliation is the test. If the $4.5bn is a run rate, IBM's expense base should show roughly that much structural reduction against 2023; if it is cumulative since 2023, the annual figure is far smaller than the headline implies. Watch whether the number is ever tied to a GAAP line, and whether the promised additional $1bn in 2026 shows up in gross margin or SG&A.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A transcripts and verbatim quotes, but two mutually inconsistent framings of the same figure from CEO and CFO, on a company-defined non-GAAP metric.

entries.claim: EVP and Chief Digital Officer Joe Inzerillo, in an interview published 3 Oct 2025: "We've been able to take about $100 million in cost out of our support function and deliver as good or better CSAT for our customers." CEO Marc Benioff, on a podcast reported 2 Sep 2025, on support headcount: "I've reduced it from 9,000 heads to about 5,000, because I need less heads." Neither figure appears in any Salesforce earnings call or SEC filing - verified against the Q4 FY26 (25 Feb 2026) and Q1 FY27 (27 May 2026) official transcripts, which contain no support-cost or support-headcount figure at all.
entries.source_name: CIO interview with Joe Inzerillo (EVP/CDO); Fortune report of Benioff podcast remarks
entries.mechanism: Agentforce deployed on Salesforce's own support organisation - deflection and autonomous resolution of inbound cases, with an SDR agent additionally reported to have processed 43,000+ leads generating $1.7m of pipeline and a service agent handling 1.4m+ conversations.
entries.shape_justification: C2, logged at Tier C on purpose, and the disclosure gap is the finding. This is the single most-cited enterprise AI cost-savings claim in circulation, and it exists only in an interview and a podcast - never in a filing, never on an earnings call, never in a document management is legally exposed on. METHOD's tier logic says exactly why that matters. Two further cautions: the widely repeated Bloomberg/Dreamforce version attributing the $100m to Benioff has no locatable verbatim, so the dollar claim is credited here to Inzerillo, who did say it on the record; and the only 2026 first-party number in this area is a productivity-hours metric - Robin Washington, Q1 FY27: Slackbot is "driving 3.8 million hours of annualized productivity gains" - which Salesforce never converts to dollars.
entries.falsifier: Salesforce reports segment margins quarterly. If ~$100m came out of support and 4,000 support roles went, the effect should be visible in cost of revenue and in total headcount - and management should eventually be willing to say so on a call. Continued absence from filings while the number circulates in the press is itself the falsification: an unaudited claim no executive will repeat under securities liability.
entries.confidence_why: Named executives and verbatim quotes, but Tier C sources, one of them a podcast, and both conspicuously absent from every first-party financial disclosure since.

entries.claim: DBS's Annual Report 2025 (published ~8 Mar 2026) states the bank has "over 2,000 models and more than 430 use cases delivering economic value of approximately SGD 1 billion." The trajectory is on record: a year earlier DBS's head of generative AI said the bank "has earned S$750 million through its use of the technology" and expected economic value "could surpass S$1 billion this year."
entries.source_name: DBS Annual Report 2025, Letter from Chairman and CEO
entries.mechanism: Roughly 430 production use cases across customer operations, credit decisioning, wealth prospecting and process automation, with the bank's own attribution model converting each to an economic-value figure.
entries.shape_justification: C4 - the cell that matters, and the largest number in it. But METHOD trap 3 applies squarely: "economic value" is a DBS-defined composite of revenue uplift, cost avoidance and loss avoidance, and DBS publishes neither the methodology nor a cost-only split. So this cannot be presented as a S$1bn cost saving; it is a S$1bn internally-attributed benefit of unknown composition. It is logged at Tier A because it appears in an audited annual report over the Chairman and CEO's names, which is a materially higher bar than the interview-grade sourcing behind most claims of this size, and because the disclosed year-on-year progression (S$750m to ~S$1bn) is the kind of series that can be tracked and falsified.
entries.falsifier: Two tests. First, whether DBS ever discloses the cost/revenue split or the attribution method - continued refusal after several years of headline growth suggests a metric built for the annual report. Second, whether the bank's cost-to-income ratio actually improves in line with a benefit of this size relative to its expense base; if economic value compounds while cost-income is flat, the metric is not reaching the P&L.
entries.confidence_why: Annual report and verbatim, but an undefined composite metric with no published methodology and no cost-only figure.

entries.claim: Santander disclosed (22 Jun 2026) "EUR 35 million in business value generated in Q1" from AI, expected to "exceed EUR 200 million by year-end," against an Investor Day (25 Feb 2026) target of "more than EUR 1 billion of business value annually (cost savings plus revenues) from data and AI initiatives" by 2028, "contributing around 1 percentage point of the group's cost-to-income improvement." Operational detail: a Brazilian card-fraud claims process made "around 95% faster, with up to 90% automation and an error rate below 1%."
entries.source_name: Santander corporate news page + 2026 Investor Day press release
entries.mechanism: Contact-centre self-service, fraud-claims automation and AML alert processing across a 185,000-employee base. Named targets include ~240,000 UK voice calls (40% of annual volume) resolved through self-service, giving "service teams around 45,000 hours back," and Openbank AI models processing ~100,000 AML alerts per year.
entries.shape_justification: C4. Trap 3 again, and Santander is at least explicit about it - "business value" is defined in its own words as "cost savings plus revenues," so the cost share of the EUR 35m and the EUR 1bn is unknown. Logged because of one unusually falsifiable feature: Santander tied the programme to a specific, auditable financial target - about 1 percentage point of cost-to-income improvement - which almost no company does. That converts a soft claim into a checkable one. The widely reported "EUR 500m+ cost reduction / GBP 433m" split appears only in wire coverage, not in Santander's own text, and is deliberately excluded here.
entries.falsifier: The cost-to-income ratio. A ~1pp improvement attributed to data and AI by 2028 is a hard, published, auditable number - if the ratio does not move by roughly that much, or moves for unrelated reasons management then credits to AI, the claim fails. Interim test: does the promised EUR 200m+ for FY26 get confirmed with a figure in the annual report rather than a corporate news page?
entries.confidence_why: Company-issued but Tier B (story page plus Investor Day release, not a filing), and a composite metric - offset by an unusually specific and checkable cost-to-income commitment.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (14 Jul 2026) Jamie Dimon said: "We have had discrete areas where we did reduce jobs by 30% or 40%, and most of those people offered jobs elsewhere," alongside "almost 1,000 use cases today." At the 2025 Investor Day, Marianne Lake guided that "headcount will trend down by about 10% over the next five years or so, even as the business grows by another more than 25%," and Jeremy Barnum said "our investments in AI/ML delivered a 35% increase in value last year." No dollar figure, no named units, and no absolute headcount were disclosed.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript) + 2025 Investor Day official transcript
entries.mechanism: Roughly 1,000 use cases with about 50 described as material, across risk, fraud, marketing, hedging, prospecting, note-taking, idea generation and document reading. The headcount effect is concentrated in operations, where Lake noted ops headcount grew only 13% over five years against 25%+ business growth.
entries.shape_justification: C4, and the most concrete headcount claim from any non-tech incumbent found so far: a named CEO stating realized 30-40% job reductions in specific (unnamed) areas. Two hard caveats. Barnum's "35% increase in value" is a growth rate off an undisclosed base and is NOT a dollar figure - the $1-1.5bn and $2bn AI-value numbers circulating for JPMorgan did not appear in any 2026 primary document checked and are excluded. And Dimon in the same breath argues against the durable-margin thesis this ledger might otherwise be read as supporting: "the ultimate beneficiary of AI will be our customers," "the benefit accrues to the customer, not to JPMorgan," "AI will have its gives and takes. We can't project." That is the CEO of the largest US bank predicting AI cost gains are competed away into price - the single most important qualification in this ledger.
entries.falsifier: The -10% headcount-over-five-years guide is the falsifier, and it is public and dated. If total headcount is flat or up by 2030 while the business grows, the operations reduction was reallocation rather than structural. Dimon's own competed-away thesis predicts exactly that outcome in the financials: efficiency delivered to customers, not to the expense line.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A transcript plus first-party Investor Day PDF; quotes verbatim. Confidence is in the statements, not in a dollar - JPMorgan disclosed none.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (16 Jul 2026) UnitedHealth disclosed that AI has "year to date... processed about half a million prior auths and saved 69,000 administrative hours," with "96% first-pass approval for digital prior authorizations." Optum's Patrick Conway said ambient listening is "available to 70% of our employed providers today and on track to exceed 90% by year-end" and that "patient access has expanded by nearly 200,000 more patient-facing hours." Forward commitments include $3bn of AI investment through 2027 and eliminating 30% of total prior-auth volume by end-2026.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript)
entries.mechanism: AI adjudication of prior authorisations at Optum Insight, plus ambient clinical documentation across employed providers - the two highest-volume administrative processes in US healthcare.
entries.shape_justification: C4, and structurally the most interesting entry in this ledger because the metric is hours, not dollars, and UnitedHealth offers no cost-per-hour conversion. 69,000 hours is roughly 33 FTE-years - against a company of ~400,000 people, which is why the honest read is that this is an early-innings figure and not yet a margin event. Logged anyway because prior authorisation is exactly the kind of high-volume, rule-bound administrative work where AI cost effects should appear first and most measurably, so the series is worth tracking from a low base. The ambient-listening figure is capacity creation (more patient-facing hours), i.e. C4-shaped input, not a saving.
entries.falsifier: The 30%-of-prior-auth-volume-eliminated-by-end-2026 target is dated, specific and checkable. Also watch whether the hours metric is ever converted to dollars or into the medical/operating cost ratio - and whether $3bn of AI investment through 2027 produces a disclosed return, since at 69,000 hours a year the arithmetic does not close yet.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A transcript, specific verified figures, and the company's own framing is appropriately modest. The uncertainty is about magnitude, which is stated, not about the numbers.

entries.company: NBER Working Paper 34836 - 'Firm Data on AI' (~6,000 executives, 4 countries)
entries.claim: Survey of ~6,000 executives across four countries, fielded Nov 2025 - Jan 2026: "More than 90 percent of executives report no effect of AI use on employment over the past three years" and "89 percent report no impact on labor productivity." Among the minority reporting an effect, the "estimated average boost of 0.29 percent." Forward expectations are also small: AI "will increase labor productivity by 1.4 percent on average while reducing employment by 0.7 percent."
entries.source_name: NBER Working Paper 34836 (authors incl. Yotzov, Barrero, Bloom, Bunn, Davis, Mizen, Thwaites), via NBER Digest
entries.mechanism: Firm-level executive survey measuring realized effects on employment and labour productivity over a three-year window, rather than sentiment about AI's promise.
entries.shape_justification: C4 as the modal respondent (non-tech, non-engineering), though the finding spans all four cells and should be read against every one of them. This is the most important entry in the ledger and it cuts against it: at the population level, the effects this ledger records at named large firms are not visible. Distinguished from the consultant surveys METHOD rejects because it measures realized outcomes rather than expectations, is authored by identifiable academic economists, and reports its own null result. The obvious reconciliation - and the load-bearing assumption to interrogate - is selection: the log records the small tail of firms that both achieved something and chose to publish it. Co-author Gregory Thwaites: "80% of the time, neither of those things seem to have changed much... But the answer is very much 'yet.'"
entries.falsifier: A later wave of the same instrument showing the no-effect share falling materially below 90%. That is the cleanest available test of whether the tail is spreading to the mean or staying a tail - and it is the number that would change this log's overall verdict more than any single corporate disclosure.
entries.confidence_why: Large multi-country sample, credible authorship, measures realized rather than anticipated effects, and reports a null - the least incentive-compatible result to publish.

entries.claim: At its 1H FY26 results briefing (19 Feb 2026) Telstra reported underlying labour costs down 9% (-A$181m), more than 1,000 roles cut in the half and 2,356 in CY2025, with headcount down 7% - and CEO Vicki Brady "could not point to a specific role that AI has directly replaced so far." CFO Michael Ackland: "There is a risk here that you end up in software licencing, cloud cost and in paying the AI providers so that you offset your benefits."
entries.source_name: Results briefing coverage (iTnews, CFOtech) of 1H FY26 results
entries.mechanism: Large realized labour-cost reduction delivered by restructuring, in a company simultaneously running a substantial AI programme - and explicitly declining to connect the two.
entries.shape_justification: C4 counter-evidence, and the cleanest example in either ledger of the pattern this log keeps meeting from the other direction: real savings, real AI programme, and management refusing to join them. It is the cost-side twin of UPS (logged 28 Jul), which attributed A$-scale transformation benefits to network reconfiguration with no AI attribution anywhere. Ackland's warning is the run-cost offset (METHOD trap 6) stated by a CFO on the record, and group executive Kim Krogh Andersen put it more sharply: "we will actually see the run cost of AI outperform the benefits of AI" without the right foundation. Any AI cost thesis has to price this objection; almost no vendor case study does.
entries.falsifier: If a future Telstra result does attribute a labour or cost line to AI with a figure, this entry weakens. If successive halves keep delivering labour savings that management keeps declining to attribute, it strengthens - and the reasonable inference becomes that AI-labelled savings elsewhere in this ledger are partly relabelled restructuring.
entries.confidence_why: Tier C trade-press reporting of a real results briefing with named executives quoted; the underlying A$181m and headcount figures are company-reported, the AI-attribution refusal is directly quoted.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026) CFO Jim Rogers disclosed: "The algorithm attach rate in Q2 is 45%, a slight uptick from the 40% that we had quoted in Q1" - and then removed the revenue reading himself: "Many of those algorithms remain not being paid, and so there's no impact on revenue from the number of algorithms." Q2 revenue $382.5m (+22% YoY); Diagnostics $289.3m (+20%); Data and Apps $93.2m (+28%). The company's own guided uplift - "an estimated $200 uplift in ASP, which equates to approximately $85 million on an annual basis beginning in 2027" and ~$400m by 2028 - is tied to FDA approval of tumor-only xT CDx and unified ADLT pricing, i.e. to a reimbursement event, not to the algorithms.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call transcript
entries.mechanism: AI algorithms (multi-modal models scoring pathology, imaging and molecular data) are ordered alongside a sequencing test and delivered in the report. Attach rate is the share of tests that carry at least one algorithm. The intended revenue path is per-algorithm reimbursement; that path is largely not yet open, so consumption rises while the associated revenue stays at zero.
entries.shape_justification: S1 - the disclosed number is an input metric (attach rate), not revenue. The S1 standing caveat is satisfied in the strongest possible way: the company did not merely omit the revenue conversion, the CFO volunteered that it is zero. Logged as counter-evidence against S3: this is a frontier-capability AI product, deployed at commercial scale, consumed by clinicians on 45% of tests, generating no incremental revenue - the capability gate is passed and the newly-economic gate is not. Scope is appendix: Tempus is an AI-native diagnostics company, out of scope as a revenue-log subject; it is retained as a comparator because entrants quantify what incumbents will not, and because it is the cleanest available separation of AI capability from AI monetisation.
entries.falsifier: If a later quarter shows attach rate rising further with algorithms still unpaid, the 'capability without monetisation' reading holds. It is falsified if Tempus discloses per-algorithm reimbursement revenue as a separate line, or attributes a specific dollar amount of Diagnostics revenue to algorithms rather than to ADLT/xT CDx pricing. Watch also whether the $85m 2027 and ~$400m 2028 uplifts are ever restated as algorithm-driven; today they are explicitly reimbursement-driven.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A full transcript; both figures and the disclaimer are direct CFO quotes, and the disclaimer cuts against the company's own interest.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026) CEO Rick McCathron said two named AI agents went live in the quarter - "Hannah, our AI service agent, and Clara, our AI First Notice of Loss agent, are both live this quarter" - and that "together they're a big part of why we can grow the top line without growing overhead at the same pace." CFO Guy Zeltser: "Our continued focus on operating leverage through AI enables us to grow our business while keeping fixed expense largely flat." Q2 revenue $144.7m; net expense ratio 45.4% (-8pp YoY); fixed expense ratio 29%, down 39 points since the start of 2024.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call transcript
entries.mechanism: Two customer-facing LLM agents in the non-engineering cost base: Hannah handles inbound policy service contacts, Clara takes first notice of loss. Both sit where headcount would otherwise scale with policy count, so the claimed effect is a flat fixed-expense base under a growing book rather than an expense line that falls.
entries.shape_justification: C4 - non-tech sector (a licensed home insurance carrier; revenue is premium and commission, not software) and a non-engineering function (service and claims intake). Cost ledger, not a revenue shape: management framed this as operating leverage, and no revenue is attributed to either agent. Trap 5 applies - this is cost avoidance (headcount not added), not a realized reduction, and management said so in those words. Trap 1 also present and deliberately not logged as a saving: the same call disclosed Devin, Cognition's AI software engineer, rolled out to "nearly a third of our roughly 500 employees" - an adoption metric with no outcome attached, which is why it is noted here rather than entered as a C3. The 39-point fixed-expense-ratio decline since early 2024 predates both agents and is not AI-attributable; only the Q2 flat-fixed-expense claim is.
entries.falsifier: If policy count and premium keep growing while fixed expense stays flat over the next two quarters, the operating-leverage claim holds. It fails if fixed expense resumes scaling with the book, if the expense ratio improvement reverses, or if Hannah/Clara stop being named once the growth story needs a different explanation. Also watch whether Hippo ever quantifies the two agents' contribution rather than describing it.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A transcript and named systems, but the causal claim is qualitative - the disclosed ratios are company-level and have several parents besides AI.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (28 Jul 2026) CEO Jim Farley said BlueCruise "paid subscriptions in Q2 grew by 20%" and that "BlueCruise made up 50% of our retail Integrated Services revenue"; Ford reported 1.6m total paid subscriptions, including 900,000+ Ford Pro Intelligence subscriptions "growing over 20% year-over-year".
entries.source_name: Ford Motor Q2 2026 earnings call
entries.mechanism: BlueCruise is a machine-learning-based hands-free highway driving system sold as a standalone subscription ($49.99/month, $495/year, $2,495 one-time) on top of the vehicle. Revenue is the subscription itself, attached at or after point of sale by dealers; Farley noted "our dealers are getting better at selling" it. Ford Pro Intelligence is the equivalent telematics/fleet-software subscription on the commercial side.
entries.shape_justification: S2, not S3. Test (a) counterfactual purchase: a buyer wanting hands-free highway driving could buy GM's Super Cruise or Tesla FSD, so the demand pre-exists and a competitor lost this sale. Test (b) prior alternative: a paid competitor product, not doing-without. Test (c) capability gate: FAILS decisively - BlueCruise has shipped since 2021 and Super Cruise since 2017; nothing here needs a capability that did not exist 24 months ago. Test (d) newly economic: no evidence offered. Within Ford's OWN catalog there is no predecessor SKU, which is why this reads S3-ish on first pass - that is exactly the misclassification METHOD warns about, since the test is industry-level counterfactual, not catalog-level novelty. LOAD-BEARING CAVEAT: Ford framed this as "software," not "AI," on the call; the AI characterisation is the log's, on the grounds that hands-free autonomy is a neural-network product. Discount accordingly. Also note what is NOT disclosed: no absolute dollar of Integrated Services revenue. The only absolute figure Farley gave was forward-looking - "we could absolutely see this business, the Integrated Services, being a half point of margin for the company" - which is PROJECTED, not realized.
entries.falsifier: If Q3 or Q4 2026 drops the paid-subscription growth rate and the BlueCruise share of retail Integrated Services revenue from disclosure, or if Integrated Services never appears as a named contributor in Ford's margin bridge, the 'half point of margin' was narrative. A second falsifier: subscription COUNT growth continuing while Ford still refuses to state Integrated Services revenue in dollars would suggest the base is too small to be material.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A and the growth rate and mix share are specific and management would be embarrassed to walk them back - but the absolute revenue base is undisclosed, and Ford itself did not use the word AI.

entries.claim: XPO's Q2 2026 release (30 Jul 2026) states "we continued to improve labor productivity above target by implementing new AI capabilities across the network, enhancing efficiency"; on the same day's call CEO Mario Harik credited "our workforce planning technology" with improving "productivity by nearly 2.5 points versus last year, which outperformed our quarterly target of 1.5%", and said AI trailer-loading pilots delivered "load quality improved by more than 40%, while damages were reduced by 50%".
entries.source_name: XPO Q2 2026 earnings call and results release
entries.mechanism: Two distinct systems. (1) Workforce planning: forecasting freight volume by door and shift to schedule dock and P&D labour against it, which is where the 2.5-point productivity number comes from. (2) Trailer loading: cameras photograph freight at each tier inside the trailer, a vision model scores load quality and instructs the dock worker to correct it in real time - fewer damages and more cube per trailer, i.e. fewer linehaul miles for the same freight. Rollout across the full network is planned for H2 2026.
entries.shape_justification: C4 - non-tech sector, non-engineering function (dock and P&D operations, the bulk of an LTL carrier's cost base). The reason this is a cost entry and not a revenue shape: every number is an input-cost or quality metric and no revenue, yield or price is attributed anywhere. ATTRIBUTION DRIFT worth recording, and the main reason confidence is not higher: the press release attributes above-target labour productivity to "new AI capabilities", while the transcript attributes the specific 2.5-point figure to "workforce planning technology" without saying AI. The same quarter, the same company, two primary documents, two different attributions - METHOD trap 4 (many parents) in miniature. Trap 5 also applies: this is productivity above target, not a cost line that fell; XPO's adjusted LTL operating ratio of 79.9% has network investment, pricing and fleet as co-drivers. The 40%/50% trailer-loading figures are PILOT-SITE results, not network results, and should not be read as realized.
entries.falsifier: If H2 2026 completes the network-wide trailer-loading rollout and the damage claims ratio and LTL operating ratio do not improve beyond the 0.2% and 79.9% posted this quarter, the pilot numbers did not survive scale. Second falsifier: if the Q3 or Q4 release drops the phrase attributing labour productivity to AI while the productivity target itself stays, the AI framing was decoration on a workforce-scheduling result.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A and specific, but the AI attribution and the quantified productivity figure sit in different documents and do not cleanly overlap.

entries.company: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis - 'AI and Productivity: What Firms Are Saying on Earnings Calls' (~490,000 transcripts, 5,198 US listed firms, 2000-2025)
entries.claim: St. Louis Fed research published 31 Jul 2026 (Ozkan, Kalyani, Sullivan) classifying productivity-related sentences in ~490,000 earnings call transcripts from 5,198 US listed firms finds that "approximately 95% of AI-related productivity sentences referred to future gains, compared with roughly three-fourths of non-AI-related" sentences, that "95% described productivity as increasing, and the share describing a decrease was negligible", and that AI's share of productivity-related sentences went from near zero pre-ChatGPT to "roughly 15% of productivity sentences" by end-2025.
entries.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, On the Economy
entries.mechanism: Two-step text classification over the full transcript corpus: extract productivity-related sentences, then use an open-weight model (Qwen3-3B) to label each for AI relevance, sentiment and temporal framing. Measures what management SAYS about productivity, not what productivity did.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence, tagged to the cost ledger because the subject is productivity claims. PLACEMENT CAVEAT, stated plainly: the corpus is not cut by sector or by function, so C4 is a placement of convenience following the NBER WP 34836 precedent (logged 2026-07-30) rather than a claim that the study is about non-tech non-engineering work. Why it matters more than most entries here: it quantifies the exact failure mode this log was built to detect. A 95%-future-tense rate against a ~75% baseline for non-AI productivity talk means AI productivity discussion is roughly 5x more skewed toward the unrealized than ordinary productivity discussion is, and the near-total absence of decrease-sentences means the corpus contains almost no disconfirming management commentary at all. That is a description of narrative, not of results - and it is consistent with what this log has found by hand across six runs.
entries.falsifier: If the authors extend the series through 2026-2027 and the future-tense share falls materially toward the ~75% non-AI baseline, AI productivity talk will have converted from promise to reported result and this entry becomes a dated snapshot rather than a standing objection. Conversely, a flat 95% into 2027 would make it much harder to argue the log's emptiness is a timing problem.
entries.confidence_why: Central-bank research, full-population corpus rather than a sample, transparent method; the measured object is management language, which is exactly what it claims to measure.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (23 Jul 2026) CEO Geoff Ballotti said "roughly 60% of travel searches by our guests are occurring within an LLM" and disclosed "a 20% higher conversion on our brand.com sites when the guest connects to us from an LLM." Wyndham Connect, the AI guest-engagement platform, is in over 5,000 hotels handling "260,000 guest interactions via this AI tool per day" and generates "$100,000 or more in increased revenues" for engaged franchisees; Wyndham AI Concierge, live in 1,500 hotels, delivers "up to ... 500 basis points of direct contribution" and a "15% increase in ADR, if you're booking it autonomously versus on the phone."
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript via Investing.com)
entries.mechanism: Two distinct paths. (1) Demand capture: as guest search migrates into LLMs, Wyndham converts LLM-originated traffic to brand.com at a 20% higher rate than other sources - it is winning the direct booking rather than losing the guest to an OTA. (2) Autonomous booking: the AI Concierge takes voice/SMS reservations end to end at the property, and a room booked autonomously prices 15% above the same booking taken on the phone, because the agent upsells and does not drop calls. The per-franchisee revenue figure is Wyndham's attribution for the most engaged properties, not a rolled-up corporate number.
entries.shape_justification: S2, not S3. Test: absent the AI, would this guest have booked a hotel room? Almost certainly yes - from an OTA, from a competing brand, or from the same property over the phone at a lower ADR. The mechanism is channel capture and price realisation on demand that already existed. Who lost the sale: OTAs (Booking, Expedia), competing economy/midscale brands, and Wyndham's own lower-yielding phone channel. Zero-sum at industry level and GDP-neutral - a guest who was going to sleep somewhere sleeps somewhere slightly more expensive. The 60%-of-searches-in-an-LLM figure is a channel-shift statistic, not a demand-creation one, and should not be read as new TAM.
entries.falsifier: If Q3/Q4 2026 calls repeat the per-franchisee "$100,000 or more" and the 15% ADR premium without ever converting them into a disclosed corporate fee-revenue contribution, a RevPAR index gain against the competitive set, or a direct-vs-OTA channel mix shift, this was a franchisee sales pitch rather than a company result. Also watch whether the ADR premium survives contact with the full 5,000-hotel base rather than the 1,500 Concierge properties.
entries.confidence_why: Named exec, on the record, on a Tier A call, with several hard numbers - but the revenue figure is a per-property "or more" attribution with no methodology, disclosed in the same quarter Wyndham missed on revenue. Two secondary renderings of the same disclosure disagree on detail (Investing.com's slide summary reports "4 million interactions" and "400bps customer satisfaction / 500bps voice conversion" where the transcript says 40m cumulative messages, 260k/day and "500 basis points of direct contribution"); I have used the transcript wording and flag the discrepancy. Benzinga's rendering of the same call contains none of these figures at all, which suggests at least one transcript is partial.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026) Miles Wuller, CEO of Underwriting Managers, said "the average RSUM property employee ... achieved 11% more quotes per head in the last 12 months than the prior year", attributing it to "our investments in automated data extraction, data structuring, enrichment, and rating pre-population coming to life." CEO Tim Turner said the "reinsurance FAC workbench now turns a submission into a priced decision-ready file in minutes, not days", that the firm has "started rolling out a proprietary engine for deploying AI around the firm", and that the underwriting-managers business is "auditing five times as many files as we did last year."
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript via Investing.com); corroborated by Coverager, 31 Jul 2026
entries.mechanism: Submission intake is the bottleneck in specialty underwriting: a broker sends an unstructured schedule of values, and a human keys it into a rating engine. Automated extraction, structuring, enrichment and rating pre-population removes that step, so the same headcount quotes more accounts. Capacity, not price - Wuller's framing is explicitly that efficiency is a countervailing force against a 25-35% decline in catastrophe pricing.
entries.shape_justification: S1: every disclosed number is an input metric - quotes per head, cycle time, files audited. Revenue conversion was conspicuously NOT disclosed. Management said the unlocked capacity "is being directed back into what matters most, winning new business" and that "high retention and new-business wins limited the decline in property revenue", but attached no AI-attributed revenue number to either. More quotes is not more bound premium: in a softening property market a higher quote count can simply mean more declined quotes at inadequate rates. Note also the honesty of the attribution - Wuller conceded the gain "certainly includes hustle", and the named mechanisms (data extraction, rating pre-population) are automation more than frontier AI, so the capability gate is weak even though the firm frames it inside its AI rollout.
entries.falsifier: If organic revenue growth in Underwriting Managers does not outpace the segment's headcount growth over the next two to three quarters, the 11% quote-per-head gain was absorbed by rate declines and lost quotes rather than converted into premium. A second tell: if the quotes-per-head metric is not repeated next year, it was a one-off talking point.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call, named executive, precise figure, and independently reported by Coverager the following day with identical wording. Marked down because the metric is self-defined ("quotes per head" over an unstated denominator of property employees), the speaker himself partly attributes it to effort rather than tooling, and no revenue conversion is offered.

entries.company: BIS Working Paper 1325 - 'AI adoption, productivity and employment: evidence from European firms' (12,000+ non-financial EU/US firms)
entries.claim: Instrumental-variables study of matched EIBIS-ORBIS data on "more than 12,000 non-financial firms in the European Union (EU) and United States (US)", instrumenting EU firms' AI adoption with the adoption rates of matched US peers: "AI adoption increases the level of labor productivity by 4%." The authors find "no adverse effects on firm-level employment", attribute the gain to capital deepening, and find the benefit concentrated in medium and large firms.
entries.source_name: BIS Working Paper No. 1325 (Aldasoro, Gambacorta, Pal, Revoltella, Weiss, Wolski)
entries.mechanism: Not a deployment finding - a causal estimate of the effect size the rest of this ledger is trying to measure one company at a time. Uses matched US peer adoption as an instrument to break the endogeneity between being a good firm and adopting AI, which is the flaw in every cross-sectional adoption-vs-performance correlation.
entries.shape_justification: C4: sample is non-financial firms, effect measured at the whole-firm level rather than in an engineering function. Logged as cost/productivity, not revenue - the outcome is labor productivity, and the paper explicitly attributes it to capital deepening rather than to new demand, so nothing here supports S1-S3. Its value is as a magnitude check: 4% is one to two orders of magnitude below the 30-40% self-reported gains sitting elsewhere in this ledger (Amex, BNY), and it is the only causally identified estimate in the ledger. Backlog entry, not fresh news - published 23 Jan 2026 and logged now because the C ledger otherwise contains only surveys and text-mining and was missing its best-identified datapoint. Age is stated so nobody reads it as a new disclosure.
entries.falsifier: The instrument assumes US peer adoption affects EU firm outcomes only through EU adoption; if AI adoption by US peers hits EU firms through competition or supply chains, the estimate is biased. Falsified if later vintages of EIBIS with post-2024 frontier-model adoption fail to reproduce a positive productivity effect, or if the 4% shrinks toward zero once the pre-generative-AI adopters are dropped from the sample.
entries.confidence_why: Central-bank working paper with a plausible identification strategy and a large sample, but not peer reviewed, and the adoption measure is survey-reported and largely pre-dates frontier generative models - so 4% is likely an estimate of the older ML wave, not of what firms are buying in 2026.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026) WTW launched programme 'Propel', committing to spend "approximately $625 million in cash" plus "approximately $25 million in non-cash charges to produce approximately $400 million in run-rate savings" by the end of 2028, from "embedding AI and automation across our business" (CEO Carl Hess). CFO Andrew Krasner tied it to "2028 adjusted operating margin targets of 30% at the enterprise, 35% in HWC, and 30% in R&B". No revenue uplift was quantified: asked where growth comes from, Krasner said "the growth comes from how we redeploy that capacity that gets generated over time."
entries.source_name: WTW Q2 2026 earnings call transcript
entries.mechanism: Broking and HWC workflow automation - the named live tools are Navigator and Neuron, described as "not pilots, they're live and in daily use" - plus process automation across a labour-heavy advisory cost base. The saving is headcount and process cost in client-facing and support functions, not engineering.
entries.shape_justification: C4: non-tech (insurance broking and HR/benefits advisory), non-engineering function - the cost base being attacked is broking and consulting labour. Not a revenue shape at any point: WTW quantified the spend, the saving and the margin target, and explicitly declined to quantify a revenue uplift, routing it instead through capacity redeployment. That is METHOD trap 2 in partial form - management banks the cost saving in guidance but leaves the revenue leg entirely qualitative. Note also the ratio: $625m of cash out to get $400m of annual run-rate saving is a ~1.6x payback-year gross, i.e. the run-cost offset is being paid up front and disclosed, which is rarer and better than most cost claims in this ledger.
entries.falsifier: If FY2027 and FY2028 do not show adjusted operating margin marching toward 30% at the enterprise level, or if the $400m run-rate saving is restated downward or quietly folded into a generic 'transformation' bucket without an AI attribution, this was a re-labelled restructuring programme. Second falsifier: organic revenue growth staying at or below mid-single digits through 2028 would confirm the redeployment leg never converted.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A, specific, dated, and management-owned with a hard 2028 checkpoint - but entirely forward-looking, and $625m of restructuring spend with an AI label is exactly the disclosure METHOD trap 4 warns about.

entries.claim: In H1 2026 results (30 Jul 2026) TP disclosed "the number of AI projects running in production reaching 1,100+ in Q2 2026", up 2.3x, with 272 new AI projects launched in Q2 alone, and said "the AI and efficiency program is expected to generate annual run-rate savings of EUR 150-170 million, with half of these benefits to be realized in 2026." On the call management attributed roughly EUR 50-70 million of that total to "applying AI to our core operations" - recruiting, quality assurance and workforce management. EBITDA margin was flat year over year.
entries.source_name: TP H1 2026 results presentation and earnings call
entries.mechanism: AI applied to TP's own internal delivery cost base - candidate screening and recruiting, automated QA of agent interactions, and workforce/schedule management across a several-hundred-thousand-person delivery workforce.
entries.shape_justification: C4: non-tech (business process outsourcing), non-engineering function.
