Logged once, in the cost ledger, per the single-ledger rule: TP also disclosed a financial-services win projected at "EUR 15-20 million in revenue during H2 2026" and said strategic lines are "more than 15% of Core Services revenue", but that is TP selling AI-enabled services - shovel revenue, out of scope as a revenue subject - and the number the disclosure is actually about is the saving. Two standing traps apply: the 1,100 projects figure is an adoption metric, not a cost metric (trap 1), and the EUR 150-170m is a composite 'AI and efficiency' programme from which management carved out an AI share only verbally (trap 3). Flat YoY EBITDA margin is the tell that none of it has landed yet.
entries.falsifier: If FY2026 does not show roughly EUR 75-85m of the programme realized, or if EBITDA margin is still flat in FY2026 with the shortfall explained by pricing, the saving was competed away to clients rather than retained - which for a BPO is the live question, not whether the saving exists.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A and specific on the programme total, but the AI-attributed slice (EUR 50-70m of EUR 150-170m) is a verbal carve-out from a composite, and I read the H1 slides via Investing.com's coverage rather than the company PDF.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026) Baldwin disclosed "47 thousand tasks completed via AI over the past 17 weeks, maintaining a quality rate exceeding 99%" across "27 processes already optimized", and gave one fully specified realized saving: direct bill reconciliation "reduced run rate costs from $3 million to $1 million a year", with "internal labor cost on the process from $1.2 million to roughly $400 thousand", while reconciliation quality improved "from roughly 90% in month to a sustained 98%". Management said the model is "running at production scale, not pilot scale" and that AI benefits are embedded in the numbers via efficiency; no revenue figure was attributed to AI.
entries.source_name: Baldwin Insurance Group Q2 2026 earnings call transcript
entries.mechanism: Agentic automation of insurance-brokerage back office - matching carrier direct-bill statements to commission records, plus 26 other service-line processes across commercial and benefits.
entries.shape_justification: C4: non-tech (insurance distribution), non-engineering function - brokerage operations labour. This is the most methodologically clean cost entry in the ledger to date because it is realized rather than projected, names the specific process, and gives a before-and-after on a single line item rather than a composite. It is also the entry that shows the size problem most clearly: a $2m annual run-rate reduction at a company with roughly $1.4bn of annual revenue is about 15 basis points. Rule 1 applies to the headline: '47,000 tasks' is an adoption metric and says nothing about cost.
entries.falsifier: If the count of optimized processes is still ~27 at Q2 2027, the deployment was a one-off rather than a compounding programme. Second falsifier: if Baldwin never converts any of the freed capacity into a disclosed organic-growth or margin number, the $2m stays a rounding error and the 47,000-task headline was the point.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A, realized not projected, named process, explicit before-and-after dollars, and management volunteered the modesty of it rather than aggregating into a 'value' number.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026) CCC disclosed "over $120 million of annualized revenue from AI-based solutions that are growing at nearly 50% year-over-year", representing "approximately 11% of total revenue in the second quarter and growing approximately 45% year-over-year", and said "revenue from AI-based solutions contributed 4 points of growth", driven by APD, subrogation and EvolutionIQ. Named deployments: "a top five insurer became its largest carrier to date to adopt the AI-powered subrogation solution", and "two top five insurers expanded their use of AI-enabled claims workflows by deploying the First Look solution to identify total losses earlier".
entries.source_name: CCC Intelligent Solutions Q2 2026 earnings call transcript
entries.mechanism: Computer-vision damage appraisal and AI claims workflow sold as add-on modules into CCC's existing installed base of auto insurers and collision repairers - subrogation demand packaging, early total-loss identification, and medical-claim synthesis via the acquired EvolutionIQ technology.
entries.shape_justification: Appendix: the subject is a software vendor, out of scope for the main revenue log - CCC's AI revenue is its own sales, not adoption ROI at the deploying carriers. Shape S2, not S3, and the distinction is the point: these are add-on modules sold into an installed base that already buys CCC's claims platform, and the work displaced was either a competitor's tool or the carrier's own unpaid manual staff time. Test (a) fails - absent CCC's AI the carriers would still be processing subrogation and total losses, and paying somebody to do it. Test (c) is arguable for the vision models but not established by the source. The genuinely useful reading is the asymmetry: the quantified AI revenue sits at the vendor, and the carriers deploying it - all named only as 'top five insurers' - have disclosed no corresponding revenue or loss-ratio number of their own. That is the shape of this entire log in one disclosure.
entries.falsifier: If the ~50% YoY growth in AI-solution revenue decelerates toward CCC's ~7-8% overall growth rate within four quarters, the AI line was a re-labelling of existing modules rather than a new attach. Separately: if any named top-five carrier later discloses a quantified claims-cost or cycle-time benefit, this entry becomes the vendor half of a matched pair and the deploying-side number can finally be tested.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A, specific, dated, repeated across two framings (dollar and percentage) that reconcile with each other; the only softness is that 'AI-based solutions' is a company-defined revenue category.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (5 Aug 2026) CEO Andrew Robinson described "bionic underwriting" - "this idea of being able to automate the ingestion of everything that is submission related" - and disclosed "40% faster submissions to underwriters, 35% improvement in speed to quote." He added that "half of our underwriting is benefiting from machine learning and predictive analytics," and described SkyScore, which "allows us to ingest all financial information without any human intervention to score every principal on 10 different dimensions" in Surety.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript via Investing.com)
entries.mechanism: Submission intake in E&S is the binding constraint on premium: an underwriter can only quote what reaches the desk in a usable form. Automating ingestion of broker submissions raises the number of risks an underwriter sees per day and shortens time-to-quote, which in a broker-intermediated market raises the probability of being the first quote back and therefore the hit ratio. SkyScore extends the same logic into Surety by machine-scoring the principal's financials rather than queueing them for a human credit analyst.
entries.shape_justification: S1: every disclosed number is an input metric - submission speed, speed to quote, share of underwriting touched by ML. No premium dollar is attributed to any of it. Revenue conversion is CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT and the absence is unusually clean: gross written premium grew 13% year over year on the same call and management attributed that growth to business mix and market diversification (A&H, Agriculture, Credit & Surety) and to underwriting discipline - not to AI. The only financial line management did connect to AI was the expense ratio, which improved 2.7 points to 24.3%. Per METHOD's one-disclosure-one-ledger rule this is logged once, in the revenue ledger, because the 40%/35% throughput figures are what the entry is about; the expense-ratio reading is noted here rather than double-logged as C4.
entries.falsifier: If Q3 and Q4 2026 repeat the throughput percentages without ever disclosing a hit ratio, a submission-count-to-bound-premium conversion, or premium growth management is willing to attribute to underwriting technology, then bionic underwriting is an expense-ratio story wearing a growth story's clothes. Specifically: watch whether the 40%/35% figures reappear alongside a quote or bind volume, or whether they migrate permanently into the expense-ratio discussion.
entries.confidence_why: Named CEO, on the record, Tier A call, hard percentages - but I verified the wording against a transcript aggregator rather than Skyward's own audio or 8-K, and the numbers are management's own internal measurement with no stated baseline or methodology.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (4 Aug 2026) CFO Ewout Steenbergen said "traffic from large language models remains below 1% of room nights," adding it "hasn't moved so much recently" and represents "no material change over the last few months or quarters." Asked to quantify conversion or satisfaction gains from Priceline's agentic assistant Penny, CEO Glenn Fogel declined: "it's still very small, and we're not at a stage we're going to start giving away percentages." The only quantified AI benefit disclosed was cost - customer service cost per booking falling at a double-digit rate - against AI expense running at "a low single-digit level of our overall technology spend."
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript via Investing.com)
entries.mechanism: None - this is the absence of a mechanism. The claimed path (guests discover and book travel inside an LLM, so whoever wins the agentic channel wins the demand) is measured here at the point where it would show up in the P&L, room nights, and it is under 1% and flat.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence tagged to S2. It contradicts the channel-capture thesis logged for Wyndham on 2026-08-02, where CEO Geoff Ballotti said "roughly 60% of travel searches by our guests are occurring within an LLM" with "a 20% higher conversion on our brand.com sites when the guest connects to us from an LLM." These are not formally the same metric - searches by one franchisor's guests is not room nights across the world's largest OTA - but they are the same claim measured at two points, and the harder number is the small one. The mismatch is the finding: the LLM channel is loud upstream in search and negligible downstream in bookings. Note also that Booking is the incumbent with the most to lose from agentic disintermediation and therefore an incentive to describe the channel as small; that cuts against the disclosure, and is why the flat trend statement matters more than the level.
entries.falsifier: If Q3 or Q4 2026 shows LLM-originated room nights crossing 1% and accelerating, or Booking starts disclosing agentic conversion percentages it refused to give here, the channel is real and this entry is the wrong read. Conversely, if the sub-1% figure quietly stops being disclosed while agentic partnerships are still being announced, that is the tell in the other direction.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call, CFO on the record, a specific bound on the number - but verified via a transcript aggregator rather than Booking's own filing, and "below 1% of room nights" is a ceiling, not a measurement.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (5 Aug 2026) CEO Ariane Gorin described Vrbo's natural-language search and Property Expert agent as developments that are not driving conversion yet, saying of them: "what we're finding is that you get over 60% more information about traveler intent, and that allows us to deepen the relationships with the traveler." She drew an explicit line between AI that pays now - ranking, recommendations, personalising the UX - and consumer-facing generative features whose benefit is framed as compounding over time rather than realised.
entries.source_name: PhocusWire, "Expedia Group is investing in AI that doesn't convert yet"
entries.mechanism: The claimed S2 mechanism - a conversational front end converts browsers into bookers better than a search box - is being measured by Expedia and is not showing up in conversion. What it does produce is intent data, an input to future ranking and personalisation, which is a bet on a later conversion gain rather than a present one.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence tagged to S2. This is the most useful kind of disclosure in this log: a CEO with every incentive to claim an AI conversion win, in the quarter she raised outlook, volunteering that the flagship consumer AI features are not converting. The "over 60% more information about traveler intent" figure is a denominator game by METHOD's own definition - more data collected is not revenue - and she does not present it as one. Note the countervailing detail: the same coverage says AI-powered personalisation helped drive "record attach rates" for the Expedia brand with no number attached, so the company is not disowning AI, it is separating the part that works from the part that does not.
entries.falsifier: If Q3 or Q4 2026 discloses a conversion lift from natural-language search or Property Expert, this reads as an early-stage timing statement rather than a null. If instead these features stop being discussed while intent-data framing persists, the null hardened.
entries.confidence_why: The "over 60% more information about traveler intent" clause is verbatim-confirmed in the trade-press rendering I fetched; the "not driving conversion" characterisation is that outlet's reported speech, not a verbatim sentence I could confirm. I have not read the primary transcript, so this is logged Tier C rather than A.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (5 Aug 2026) CEO Jeremy Wacksman said: "Consumers who use AI mode spend more than three times as long on Zillow, view more than twice as many homes, run nearly three times as many searches - and contact an agent at nearly three times the rate of consumers who don't use AI mode." AI mode is live for roughly 20% of signed-in users. Q2 revenue was $772m, up 18%, and none of it was attributed to AI mode.
entries.source_name: HousingWire, Zillow Q2 2026 earnings (call 5 Aug 2026)
entries.mechanism: Agent contacts are the unit Zillow sells: Premier Agent revenue is a function of connection volume and price per connection. A conversational search mode that triples the contact rate per user is, mechanically, a Premier Agent inventory expansion - if the effect is causal.
entries.shape_justification: S1: every number is an engagement input, none is revenue. Revenue conversion is conspicuously absent - 18% revenue growth was not tied to AI mode, and no connection-volume dollar impact was given. The severe caveat, which management did not address: this is a self-selection statistic. The consumer who opts into AI mode is the high-intent consumer who was always going to contact an agent. No holdout, no control, no causal claim was offered. Logged at low confidence for exactly that reason, and it is the cleanest current example of the AI engagement metric that looks like a revenue mechanism and may be a sorting artefact.
entries.falsifier: If Zillow rolls AI mode past ~20% of signed-in users toward the full base and the 3x contact-rate multiple collapses toward 1x, the original figure was selection, not lift. Equally, if Premier Agent connection volume or revenue per visitor never inflects while AI-mode penetration triples, the mechanism does not convert.
entries.confidence_why: The quote is verbatim-confirmed across two independent renderings, but the statistic is uncontrolled and self-selected, and the marketplace's own revenue growth was pointedly not attributed to it. A 3x with no holdout is not evidence of a 3x effect.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (6 Aug 2026) CEO Brian Chesky said "In Q2, customer support costs per booking declined about 16% year-over-year, driven in part by improvements by our AI assistant" and "Nearly 45% of issues that start with our AI assistant are now resolved without a human agent." CFO Ellie Mertz repeated the figure: "The customer service cost per booking is down about 16% year-over-year, in large part due to the AI agent." No revenue was attributed to AI; the consumer-facing AI search product is still only entering test.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript via Investing.com); figures corroborated by TechCrunch, 7 Aug 2026
entries.mechanism: An AI support agent now handles first-line guest and host contacts in more than 50 languages and closes nearly half of them without a human, so the support cost carried by each booking falls. The metric is a unit cost per booking, not an absolute expense line, which means it improves both when support gets cheaper and when bookings grow faster than support cost.
entries.shape_justification: C4 - non-tech (GICS Consumer Discretionary, hotels/leisure; the same classification under which this log treats Booking, Expedia and Wyndham as in-scope) and a non-engineering function. Cost ledger, not revenue: Chesky called AI "the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb" but attached no revenue, conversion or booking number to it, and AI search is still pre-launch. The same call produced two engineering claims - concept-to-launch time down "as much as 60%" and features shipped up "nearly 80%" versus the same six months last year - which are standing trap 1, adoption and output dressed as saving: no headcount or dollar figure was banked against either, and management framed them as doing more, not spending less. Logged once, on the number that is actually a cost.
entries.falsifier: Support cost per booking stops being disclosed, or stops falling, in Q3/Q4 2026 - or the 16% turns out to be denominator-driven (bookings growing faster than support spend) rather than a lower support cost. Ask on the next call whether absolute support expense fell.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call, two executives independently repeating the number, but hedged as "driven in part" / "in large part" and expressed per booking rather than as an absolute expense.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (10 Aug 2026) CTO Mo Elshenawy said "We are making AI load-bearing, not decorative", that "Hers customers using the new care experience are sending 3 times as many messages on the platform, with AI answering 80% of their questions", and that "AI has reduced non-clinical tasks... by nearly 50%." CFO Yemi Okupe said "AI investments will pay back within 12 to 18 months" - i.e. the saving is projected, not banked. Revenue of $753m (+40%) and 300,000 net new subscribers were attributed to weight-loss expansion and the Eucalyptus acquisition, not to AI.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript via Investing.com); 8-K earnings release, 10 Aug 2026
entries.mechanism: An agentic support layer bounded by clinical protocols answers the routine share of patient messages, so clinicians and support staff absorb a 3x rise in message volume without a proportional rise in labour. The claim is a reduction in non-clinical task load, not a reduction in an expense line.
entries.shape_justification: C4 - non-tech (consumer telehealth) and a non-engineering function, the cell that matters. Standing trap 5 applies squarely: "non-clinical tasks down nearly 50%" is task load, not a realized expense reduction, and the CFO's own 12-to-18-month payback framing concedes the saving has not yet arrived. Deliberately not logged as S2: Okupe said "AI investments on our platform are driving a meaningfully better consumer experience resulting in a reduction in cancellations" - the correct revenue mechanism (churn) with no magnitude attached, which is the same test Instacart failed on 6 Aug. One disclosure, one ledger: logged where the number is.
entries.falsifier: The 12-to-18-month payback window closes (by roughly Q4 2027) without gross margin, support cost per subscriber, or an absolute opex line moving - or the cancellation improvement is never quantified. Also falsified if the 3x message volume turns out to raise clinical cost faster than AI removes non-clinical cost.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call with specific percentages, but the metrics are task-load and containment rates rather than money, and management explicitly says payback is still ahead.

entries.claim: On the H1 2026 results and 'Accelerate 2030' strategy update call (30 Jul 2026) CEO Charlie Nunn said Lloyds expects "more than 100 million pounds of value from generative and agentic AI in 2026", and the CFO guided "around GBP 2 billion of gross cost savings from 2027-2030" from an AI-led efficiency programme. Nunn also said AI would deliver "substantial benefits driving our revenue growth and efficiency in Accelerate 2030" - with no revenue number attached to it. Lloyds separately reported ~800 live AI models and a plan to train 100% of colleagues in AI by end-2026.
entries.source_name: H1 2026 results and Accelerate 2030 strategy update call (transcript via Investing.com); RTE report of the same briefing
entries.mechanism: Agentic AI agents deployed across customer service and internal operations; AI-powered credit decisions ('speed and quality'); automation of manual processes named as fraud and complaints; AI coding tools in engineering. The CFO frames the payoff as a "significant improvement in the number of active customers served per customer-facing colleague" - i.e. output per head in the branch/contact-centre estate, not in engineering, which is why this is C4 rather than C3.
entries.shape_justification: Cost ledger, C4: non-tech subject (a UK retail and commercial bank) and the savings span customer operations, fraud, complaints and back office rather than software engineering. Standing trap 3 applies squarely to the GBP 100m: Lloyds calls it 'value' and does not say what it contains - cost avoided, loss avoided or revenue - and the same undefined construct was used for the ~GBP 50m claimed for 2025 (press release, 29 Jan 2026, retrieved this run). Trap 4-adjacent on the GBP 2bn: it is 'gross cost savings' for an entire four-year strategy in which AI is the headline lever but not the only one; RTE quotes Nunn as "technology such as AI", which is looser than the AI-only framing in the trade coverage. Logged once, in the cost ledger, because that is where the numbers sit; the revenue claim is qualitative.
entries.falsifier: FY2026 results (Feb 2027) not restating an AI 'value' figure of at least GBP 100m, or restating it without ever defining what the construct contains; and the 2027-2030 GBP 2bn gross saving failing to appear as a tracked, separately reported line in subsequent results.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A management guidance with dated, falsifiable checkpoints, but both figures are forward-looking and the 'value' construct is undefined.

entries.claim: Admiral's H1 2026 results presentation (6 Aug 2026) discloses ">80% of code now generated with AI support in the UK" and "Further expansion of Predictive AI capability: 117 live models (+13% vs. YE); real-time models more than doubled". No cost, expense-ratio or revenue figure is attached to either. On the call the CEO called predictive AI "one of our biggest source of competitive advantage, with more models in production and better performance from them" and quantified only training inputs: "more than 10,000 hours of data and AI training in H1" and "a community of over 1,000 people".
entries.source_name: 2026 Half Year results presentation, 6 Aug 2026 (text extracted from the primary PDF this run); H1 2026 earnings call transcript via Investing.com
entries.mechanism: AI coding assistance embedded across the software development lifecycle in UK operations; predictive models used in pricing, risk selection and claims; GenAI scaled into claims and customer communication including voice-to-voice, live in Admiral Money and Italy.
entries.shape_justification: Cost ledger, C3: non-tech subject (a motor insurer), engineering function. Standing trap 1 in full force - '>80% of code generated with AI support' is an adoption metric, not a saving. It says nothing about cost per unit of output, headcount, or technology spend, and Admiral attaches no financial figure to it anywhere in the deck or on the call. Logged because it is a specific number from a Tier A primary document and because it is the highest AI-coding-adoption figure disclosed by a non-tech incumbent anywhere in this log - the comparators are Alphabet's 75% (C1, a tech subject) and BNY's share of engineers using the tools. METHOD's own warning applies: a coding gain on a small slice of an insurer's cost base is not a margin event, and H1 profit before tax fell 18% to GBP 429.2m on the UK motor cycle.
entries.falsifier: The expense ratio or technology cost line failing to move across FY26 and FY27 while the AI-coded share of code rises further; or the metric quietly disappearing from the FY26 results presentation (Mar 2027).
entries.confidence_why: Figure taken verbatim from the primary results deck retrieved and text-extracted this run, but it measures adoption, not cost.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026) CEO Andy Jassy said of Alexa for Shopping, Amazon's agentic shopping assistant, that "Over 350 million customers have used it in the last 12 months, and engagement accelerated in Q2, with active users nearly doubling and interactions up over 5x year-over-year", that in the U.S. "customers who use Alexa for Shopping spend an average of over 40% more per order than those who don't", and that "customers who've tried Alexa+ are signing up for Prime at nearly 25% higher rates". No incremental-sales dollar figure was given - two quarters after Amazon put a ~$12bn incremental annualized sales number on its AI shopping assistant.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript via The Motley Fool; cross-checked against the Investing.com transcript)
entries.mechanism: An agentic shopping assistant giving personalised recommendations, product comparisons and price history, and automating purchase through price alerts and auto-buy, sitting in front of the retail catalogue; Alexa+ as the household entry point feeding Prime signup.
entries.shape_justification: S1, not S2: the disclosed number is a cohort spend differential - an input/behavioural metric - not attributed incremental revenue. Selection bias is unaddressed and fatal to the naive reading, since engaged, high-frequency, high-spend shoppers are exactly the ones most likely to use an assistant; Amazon offers no counterfactual. Appendix scope because Amazon is a hyperscaler and out of scope as a subject in the main revenue log, but it belongs in the appendix as the sharpest available comparator: nobody in the main log has a consumer-facing AI cohort metric at this scale. The S1 standing caveat is the whole point of the entry - revenue conversion is conspicuously absent, and it was previously present. Per Modern Retail (Tier C, retrieved this run) Amazon disclosed at its February 2026 earnings that Rufus "was used by 300 million customers in 2025 and helped drive nearly $12 billion in incremental annualized sales", and Fortune (Nov 2025) quotes Jassy saying Rufus "is expected to generate over $10 billion in annual incremental sales for us". The word 'Rufus' does not appear anywhere in the Q2 2026 transcript and no dollar attribution replaces it. Confound stated plainly: no source retrieved this run confirms that Alexa for Shopping is a rebranded Rufus, so the metric basis may have changed rather than the disclosure being withdrawn.
entries.falsifier: A Q3 or Q4 2026 call again putting a dollar incremental-sales figure on the shopping assistant would restore the revenue attribution and make this entry a naming artefact; continued substitution of cohort-comparison metrics for the dollar figure confirms the downgrade.
entries.confidence_why: The quotes are Tier A and verbatim, but a cohort comparison cannot establish incrementality, and the disappearance of the dollar figure rests on one Tier C secondary plus a naming discontinuity I could not resolve.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (6 Aug 2026) CEO Tobias Hartmann said "around 20% of active searches on Cars.com are engaging with Carson", that "Carson users are 4x more likely to submit a lead", and that Carson users "accounted for nearly 30% of total leads submitted in the month of June". Total Q2 revenue rose 1% to $179.9m; marketplace revenue rose more than 7% while OEM and national advertising fell 18%. No revenue was attributed to Carson.
entries.source_name: Cars.com Q2 2026 earnings call transcript (Motley Fool); figures corroborated in StockStory and MarketBeat call coverage retrieved this run
entries.mechanism: Carson is an LLM shopping assistant inside the Cars.com marketplace. Cars.com does not sell cars; it sells lead flow and subscription packages to franchise and independent dealers. So the revenue path runs assistant engagement -> lead volume and lead quality -> dealer willingness to pay for marketplace packages (Premium Plus, the fastest-growing package in the quarter, targeted at 15% adoption by year-end). Carson sits upstream of the thing that is actually monetized, which is why the disclosed numbers are lead metrics rather than dollars.
entries.shape_justification: S1. Every disclosed figure is an input metric - engagement rate, lead-submission propensity, share of leads - and none is revenue. Revenue conversion was NOT disclosed, and the surrounding print argues against assuming it: total revenue grew 1% in the same quarter that AI-assisted leads reportedly reached ~30% of the June total. Either the lead-quality gain has not yet repriced dealer packages, or the 4x figure is largely selection - shoppers already close to submitting a lead are the ones who engage an assistant. Cars.com offers no control group, exactly as Amazon offered none for "spend 40% more per order" (logged 12 Aug). Note also that ~30% of leads is a June figure, not a Q2 figure; the quarter-level number was not given.
entries.falsifier: Marketplace revenue per dealer (ARPD) and dealer count failing to inflect over Q3-Q4 2026 while Carson engagement is reported higher again. If Carson engagement keeps climbing across two more quarters with no ARPD or dealer-count response, the 4x lead multiple is selection, not causation. Sharper falsifier: if the "30% of leads" statistic is dropped from the Q3 call while Carson is still promoted, treat it as a metric that stopped working.
entries.confidence_why: Quotes taken from a retrieved transcript and independently corroborated by two secondary renderings of the same call. Confidence is capped at medium by the uncontrolled comparison and by the mismatch between the AI metrics and a 1% revenue print.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (4 Aug 2026) CEO Sanjeev Sahni said "our AI models are effectively optimizing conversion, buyer growth and market share gains", disclosing an "approximately 15% improvement in CNC cost prediction accuracy" from a new-generation model and process-recommendation acceptance reaching "85%, driven by an upgraded context-aware AI process recommender". Marketplace revenue grew 45% YoY to $215.4m, total revenue 41% to a record $229.3m, active buyers 20% to 89,557; marketing spend fell to a record-low 3.4% of marketplace revenue.
entries.source_name: Xometry Q2 2026 earnings call transcript (Motley Fool); revenue, buyer and gross-profit figures corroborated against the company's Q2 2026 results release
entries.mechanism: Xometry quotes custom-manufactured parts instantly from an uploaded CAD file and routes the job to a supplier network, earning the spread. Pricing accuracy is therefore the P&L: underprice and gross margin is lost on the job, overprice and the quote does not convert. A 15% improvement in cost-prediction accuracy widens the band of jobs that can be quoted profitably, and the process recommender picking the right manufacturing process 85% of the time removes a human sourcing step. Sahni's framing that the pricing, sourcing and manufacturability models are "no longer independently doing" their jobs but "all interconnected" is the specific 2025-26 change.
entries.shape_justification: S1. The disclosed AI numbers are input metrics - prediction accuracy and recommendation acceptance - not revenue. The 45% marketplace growth is real and management links it verbally to the models, but no dollar of it is attributed, and buyer growth of 20% against revenue growth of 45% means most of the delta is wallet share and mix, which management did not decompose. Revenue conversion is therefore asserted, not disclosed. Explicitly NOT S3: these are better quotes for parts buyers who already buy machined parts from job shops, so absent Xometry the demand exists and someone serves it - test (a) fails. Scope call: kept in the main log rather than the appendix because Xometry's revenue is the sale of manufactured parts, not software licences; it is a distributor with an ML pricing engine, not a vendor selling AI. Reasonable people could push it to the appendix, and the ML quoting engine long predates the 24-month capability frontier.
entries.falsifier: Marketplace gross margin failing to hold or expand over Q3-Q4 2026 while cost-prediction accuracy is claimed to improve again - better pricing that does not show up in margin was not better pricing. Second falsifier: if the 15% accuracy and 85% acceptance statistics are not restated or bettered on the Q3 call, treat them as launch marketing for the model refresh rather than managed KPIs.
entries.confidence_why: Transcript retrieved directly and the financial figures cross-checked against the company release. Medium rather than high because the causal link from model accuracy to the 45% growth number is management's assertion with no decomposition offered, and because Xometry has grown fast through periods with no model refresh to point at.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (5 Aug 2026) CEO Tom Wilson introduced ALLIE - Allstate's Large Language Intelligent Ecosystem - an eight-component agentic AI platform that "will leverage Agentic AI to improve customer value, lower cost and increase growth", built on "250+ analytical models", "40+ petabytes" of data and "1.5 billion CPU compute hours". Asked to size it, Wilson said: "I can't give you specific numbers how much growth is going to do or how we can do at expenses." The platform is "not completely built or deployed". Issued applications rose 9.9% and net premiums written 2.6% in the quarter; neither was attributed to AI.
entries.source_name: Allstate Q2 2026 earnings call transcript (Motley Fool); ALLIE naming, build status and the refusal to quantify independently corroborated by Insurance Journal (7 Aug) and The Insurer (7 Aug)
entries.mechanism: ALLIE is an agent-to-agent orchestration layer over Allstate's existing model estate, intended to touch customer engagement, direct policy sales in three states, pricing accuracy and claims. The growth mechanism management gestures at is conversion and pricing precision at the quote - Allstate generates over 100 million quotes and purchases roughly 50 million leads a year, so small conversion movements are large absolute numbers. None of that is a disclosed result; it is the architecture of one.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence, tagged S2 because incremental premium won on existing auto and home products from existing consumers is the shape Allstate is implicitly claiming, and it is zero-sum - every policy Allstate writes at a better price is one Progressive, GEICO or State Farm did not write. The finding is the refusal: the CEO of a top-tier US insurer announced a named enterprise AI platform, listed compute and model counts to four significant figures, and would not put a number on either the expense or the growth benefit. The quantified metrics offered - 250 models, 40 petabytes, 1.5 billion CPU hours - are pure adoption and scale, METHOD's standing trap 1. Note the ordering in Wilson's own sentence: customer value, lower cost, then growth. Growth is third and the least specified. The 9.9% issued-application growth in the same quarter is credited to a "multifaceted approach" of affordability, product, distribution, marketing and claims - not to AI - which is attribution discipline by the company, and worth recording as such.
entries.falsifier: If Allstate attaches a dollar figure - expense-ratio points or premium - to ALLIE on the Q3 2026 or Q4 2026 call, this entry is premature and should be downgraded to an ordinary pre-announcement. If two more quarters pass with ALLIE promoted and still no number, and particularly if the expense ratio does not move, treat ALLIE as positioning. The 9.9% issued-application figure is the control: if it decays while ALLIE ships, the platform was not the growth engine.
entries.confidence_why: The refusal to quantify is directly quoted from a retrieved transcript and separately reported by two trade outlets that attended the same call. There is little interpretive room in an executive saying he cannot give specific numbers.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (5 Aug 2026) President Harley Finkelstein said "AI-driven traffic and also orders to Shopify stores tripled year-over-year in the second quarter", that new buyer orders from AI channels "are coming in at nearly twice the rate of other channels", that "AI searches powered by Catalog converted twice the rate of those using scraped data", and that "75% of AI-referred orders originated from outside the top 100 merchant categories". GMV grew 32% to $115.6bn and revenue 34% to $3.6bn. No dollar amount of revenue was attributed to AI; management called AI "small relative to our massive GMV".
entries.source_name: Shopify Q2 2026 earnings call transcript (Motley Fool)
entries.mechanism: LLM assistants answer a shopping intent in natural language and resolve it against structured product data. Shopify's Catalog exposes its merchants' inventory to those assistants in machine-readable form rather than leaving them to scrape it, and the 2x conversion gap between Catalog-sourced and scraped results is the price of that structure. Because assistants match intent rather than keywords, the products they surface skew away from the categories that win search-engine auctions.
entries.shape_justification: Appendix: Shopify is a software platform and out of scope as a subject in the main revenue log. Classified S2, not S3, and the distinction is the whole point of retrieving this. The long-tail statistic - 75% of AI-referred orders outside the top 100 categories - is the strongest S3-shaped claim retrieved this run, and it still fails the tests. (a) Counterfactual purchase: not established; a buyer who finds a niche product through an assistant was in most cases going to buy something in that need-state from somebody. (b) Prior alternative: the prior alternative was keyword search, which resolved to head merchants and paid placement - so this reallocates demand from head to tail, and from Google-mediated discovery to assistant-mediated discovery. Someone lost those orders. (c) Capability gate: passes cleanly - intent-resolving assistants at consumer scale did not exist 24 months ago. (d) Newly economic: partially - discovery cost for long-tail SKUs collapsed - but Shopify discloses no evidence that total category demand rose rather than moved. Three of four tests are not met, so this is a distribution shift, not new TAM. Also note what is absent: after tripling, still no dollar figure, and an explicit management caveat that the base is small.
entries.falsifier: If Shopify quantifies AI-attributed GMV in dollars in a later quarter and the number is material, this entry understates the finding. Conversely, if AI-attributed traffic triples again in Q3 while total GMV growth stays in the low 30s, the channel is substituting for search rather than adding to demand - which is the S2 reading confirmed. Watch also whether the 75% long-tail share falls as head brands optimise for assistants; if it does, this was a temporary indexing artifact, not a structural advantage for niche merchants.
entries.confidence_why: All four statistics verified verbatim in a retrieved transcript. Medium because every figure is a ratio on an undisclosed and admittedly small base, and "AI-attributed" is Shopify's own attribution construct with no published methodology - METHOD's denominator-games rule applies.

entries.claim: Ford VP of vehicle hardware engineering Charles Poon said the company "mistakenly" believed that introducing AI and adjusting design requirements would produce a high-quality product, and that Ford has since rehired, newly hired or promoted experienced engineers into vehicle engineering to fix the resulting quality gaps - reported as approximately 300 by Fox Business (citing a Bloomberg press call) and as 350 by The Next Web (citing The Verge). Poon: "Artificial intelligence is a fantastic tool, but it's only as good as the information you use to train it." Ford subsequently topped J.D. Power's 2026 US Initial Quality Study at 152 problems per 100 vehicles.
entries.source_name: Fox Business, 29 Jun 2026, reporting a Ford press call originally covered by Bloomberg; corroborated by The Next Web, 26 Jun 2026, citing The Verge
entries.mechanism: Ford substituted AI-assisted design-requirement tooling for experienced engineering judgement in vehicle quality. The failure mode Poon describes is not that the models were bad but that the veterans who held the tacit knowledge left before it was captured, so the tools amplified weak inputs instead of catching design flaws. The correction was headcount - re-hiring senior engineers - plus, per the reporting, a large expansion of AI-powered edge-case testing running alongside the humans rather than instead of them.
entries.shape_justification: C3 - non-tech company, engineering function. Counter-evidence to the cost thesis in its strongest available form: not a study, not a survey, but a named incumbent that made the substitution, measured the result, and bought the labour back. It bears on METHOD's standing trap 4 in reverse - here the headcount action has an explicitly AI-attributed cause, stated by the executive responsible, against the company's interest. Note carefully what it does and does not prove: Ford went on to lead J.D. Power initial quality, so the end state is AI plus experienced engineers beating both prior arrangements. The refutable claim is substitution, not augmentation.
entries.falsifier: If Ford's engineering headcount falls back over FY2026-27 while quality rankings hold, the rehire was a transition cost of a substitution that ultimately worked, and this entry overstates the reversal. If Ford quantifies the cost of the rehire or of the quality failures - warranty, recall or campaign expense traced to the AI-designed period - the entry should be upgraded from anecdote to a measured loss.
entries.confidence_why: Two retrieved sources give materially different engineer counts (approximately 300 vs 350) and name different primary outlets (Bloomberg vs The Verge) for the same press call. Neither primary could be retrieved this run - theverge.com blocks this agent and the Bloomberg original is paywalled - so no single figure is verified and none is asserted here. Only Poon's quoted sentence appears verbatim in a document retrieved this run. The item is also roughly seven weeks old, outside the normal window, and is logged on the METHOD ground that counter-evidence decays slowly and this one was unlogged.

entries.claim: In its H1 2026 results release (29 Jul 2026) Indosat reported revenue of IDR30.7 trillion, up 13.1% YoY, and attributed AI-powered customer experiences directly to a revenue-per-user outcome: "These differentiated experiences helped drive a 19.9% YoY increase in data traffic and a 17.3% YoY increase in Average Revenue Per User (ARPU)", to IDR46 thousand. The named experiences are the Anti-Spam and Anti-Scam feature, Sahabat-AI, Gemini AI and Adobe Express. Mobile subscribers were flat at 93.4 million, so the ARPU gain is monetisation of an existing base rather than customer acquisition.
entries.source_name: Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison H1 2026 results release, 'Delivers Double-Digit Growth, Accelerating Its AI-Led Transformation' (reprinted in full by TelecomTV); corroborated by TNGlobal, 29 Jul 2026
entries.mechanism: Two mechanisms are mixed and the company does not split them. (1) AI-driven hyperpersonalisation of offers and pricing against a 93.4m-subscriber base - genuine deployment, and the reading that would make this a real S2. (2) Bundling third-party AI subscriptions (Gemini, Adobe Express) into mobile plans as paid add-ons - that is distribution of somebody else's AI, closer to a reseller margin than to ROI on Indosat's own AI spend. The disclosed ARPU number covers both.
entries.shape_justification: S2, not S3. Test (a): absent the AI, these subscribers were already buying mobile data from Indosat or a rival - the counterfactual purchase plainly exists. Test (b): the prior alternative was a cheaper plan from the same carrier or from Telkomsel/XLSmart, so any share gain came out of a competitor or out of the customer's own downgrade decision. Zero-sum at the Indonesian industry level and GDP-neutral: this is monetisation intensity on a flat subscriber base, not new demand. Worth logging anyway because a non-tech incumbent putting a specific revenue-per-user figure next to AI on the record is rare - most of this log's S1/S2 entries stop at input metrics.
entries.falsifier: ARPU growth decelerating below ~10% YoY in FY2026 full-year or H1 2027 results while the AI narrative is retained, or the company continuing to decline to separate hyperpersonalisation-driven ARPU from third-party AI-bundle resale revenue. Also falsifying: Indonesian peers (Telkomsel, XLSmart) posting comparable ARPU gains over the same period without an AI programme, which would make this industry price repair wearing an AI label.
entries.confidence_why: The number is real and company-issued, but no counterfactual is offered and Indonesian mobile pricing repaired industry-wide over the period; the bundled-resale component is not separated from the deployment component. Logged 17 days after release - outside the normal 48-hour window and flagged as such.

entries.company: OpenAI / Chatterji, Holtz, Rakholia, Tambe & Weeratunga - 'How Organizations Use AI: Evidence from ChatGPT' (1,500+ organizations, 17m+ messages, 417 US public-company tickers)
entries.claim: Working paper submitted 12 Aug 2026 linking ChatGPT Enterprise account records to Compustat financials for US public companies through March 2026. On the only revenue question it asks, the answer is null: "Revenue per employee is not meaningfully associated with output tokens per employee once other controls are included", and for the other usage margins "the point estimates are positive for messages per active usage week per employee and weekly active users per employee, but neither coefficient is statistically significant." Adoption runs the other way - "firms with higher revenue per employee are more likely to adopt ChatGPT Enterprise", with "a one-log-point increase in lagged revenue per employee ... associated with roughly 0.4 to 0.9 percentage points higher adoption probability."
entries.source_name: Chatterji, Holtz, Rakholia, Tambe & Weeratunga, 'How Organizations Use AI: Evidence from ChatGPT', arXiv 2608.12236 (submitted 12 Aug 2026); surfaced by Fortune, 13 Aug 2026
entries.mechanism: Not a deployment finding - a measurement of whether the revenue signal this log hunts one company at a time shows up in the largest linked enterprise-AI usage dataset that exists. 521 ticker-year observations across 417 tickers with positive message volume, fiscal years 2024-2025.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence tagged to S2, the shape that claims AI produces attributable incremental revenue at adopting firms. Read it precisely, because the headline overstates it: revenue per employee here is LAGGED - measured before adoption - so this is a cross-sectional selection regression, not a causal test of whether AI raised anyone's revenue. What it establishes is (i) high-revenue-per-employee firms adopt more, i.e. adoption is selected on prior performance, which is exactly the endogeneity that makes every adopter-outperforms-non-adopter statistic worthless, and (ii) among adopters, usage intensity carries no measurable revenue signal. The load-bearing fact is the absence: OpenAI had ChatGPT Enterprise usage linked to Compustat financials through March 2026 - the data needed to test post-adoption revenue changes - and published 69 pages of adoption, seniority and task taxonomy without that result. The strongest-incentive party with the best dataset did not produce the number.
entries.falsifier: A follow-up from these authors, or any linked-data replication, showing a positive post-adoption change in revenue per employee among ChatGPT Enterprise adopters with a credible control group. That would convert this from an absence into a rebutted claim. Conversely, if the 2026 fiscal-year panel is added and the null holds with post-adoption revenue, this entry strengthens considerably.
entries.confidence_why: Quotes verified from the arXiv full text this run, not from the press summary. Confidence is capped at medium because the paper does not test the causal question, so this is evidence about the state of the evidence base rather than about AI's true revenue effect.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (10 Aug 2026) CFO Mark Stolper said "Revenue from the EBCD program increased 16%" - RadNet's Enhanced Breast Cancer Detection, an AI second read on screening mammograms that patients buy out of pocket because payers do not reimburse it. No absolute dollar figure, adoption rate or counterfactual was given on the call.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript)
entries.mechanism: A screening mammogram is covered by insurance; the AI over-read is not. RadNet offers the patient an opt-in upcharge (priced at $75 falling to $40 during the DeepHealth study period) for Saige-DX to read the study alongside the radiologist, with a second AI pass and escalation to a second radiologist on suspicious findings. The revenue is patient cash on top of a reimbursed exam - AI inference cost is near zero per study, so the entire upcharge is incremental gross margin on a scan the company was already performing.
entries.shape_justification: (a) Counterfactual purchase - PASS. The buyer is the patient, the purchase is optional, and absent the AI there is nothing to buy: the base exam is already paid for by the payer. (b) Prior alternative - PASS. Nobody sold a consumer an AI over-read before this; the nearest analogue is a radiologist double-read, which is not a purchasable US consumer SKU. The DeepHealth RSNA 2024 analysis of 747,604 women across 10 practices recorded 23% enrolment rising to 33% in the final month and states plainly that "AI is not reimbursed" - the closest published evidence that this is net-new self-pay demand. (c) Capability gate - FAIL, and this is the honest weak point. Saige-DX is CNN-era FDA-cleared mammography AI, not a post-2024 frontier capability; 2021 technology would have worked. (d) Newly economic - PASS. A human second read cannot be delivered at $40; near-zero marginal inference cost is what opens the price point. Held at S3-CANDIDATE rather than promoted: the Q2 2026 disclosure is a growth rate with no denominator, management never framed it as incremental demand, and (c) fails outright. It is nonetheless the first entry in this log where the counterfactual purchase question has a defensible yes.
entries.falsifier: RadNet stops breaking out EBCD growth in later quarters, or discloses an absolute EBCD revenue figure so small it is immaterial to a $622.7m quarter. Ironically the other falsifier is success: if payers begin reimbursing EBCD, the self-pay counterfactual collapses and the revenue becomes ordinary reimbursed imaging - S2, not S3.
entries.confidence_why: The 16% is a verified Tier A CFO statement, but it was delivered inside a list of Digital Health product-line growth rates (prostate/neuro +13%, TechLive +38%, enterprise imaging workflow +17.3%), so it is not certain whether the EBCD line being grown is patient self-pay revenue at RadNet's own centres or licensed EBCD sold to third-party providers. That ambiguity is load-bearing for the shape and is not resolved by the transcript.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (10 Aug 2026) Digital Health CEO Kees Westdorp disclosed "$16.1 million of AI revenue, up 136% year-over-year", Digital Health revenue of "$32.4 million, up 56.5%", ARR of "$105.5 million, up 97%", and that "External ARR, revenue generated outside of RadNet, now makes up 63% of our ARR base", guiding full-year ARR to over $140m.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call and results release
entries.mechanism: An imaging provider productised the AI it built for its own reading workflow and now licenses it to competing hospitals and health systems - Diagnostic Suite, Reporting Pro, AI Studio and clinical AI models - signing approximately $21m of total contract value in the quarter. Nearly two thirds of recurring revenue now comes from outside RadNet's own centres.
entries.shape_justification: Routed to the appendix because at this segment RadNet is a software vendor, not a deploying corporation: it is selling the shovels, and METHOD excludes shovel-sellers as subjects of the revenue log even when the parent sits in an in-scope sector. Shape is S2, not S3: the hospitals buying DeepHealth were already buying imaging AI and reporting software from iCAD, Lunit, Aidoc, Sectra and Philips, so a competitor lost the sale. The interesting thing is the direction of travel - a non-tech incumbent crossing into vendor economics off its own deployment - which is exactly the comparator the appendix exists to preserve. Note the segment's adjusted EBITDA fell to $2.5m from $3.4m a year earlier on infrastructure investment: the AI vendor line is growing revenue and shrinking profit.
entries.falsifier: External ARR share stalls or reverses below 63%, or full-year ARR lands materially short of the "over $140 million" guide, indicating the external business was front-loaded rather than compounding.
entries.confidence_why: Figures appear in both the fetched results release and the fetched call transcript, and are segment-reported rather than management-defined composites.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (6 Aug 2026) CEO Jason Trevisan said "Guru-driven leads up 60% sequentially in the U.S." and that VINMax "promoted listings have sold 23% faster and received 34% more leads per day than comparable non-promoted listings"; President & COO Sam Zales said "PriceVantage bookings grew more than 50% sequentially" and that adopting dealers "saw a median 15% lift in VDPs and 9% lift in leads per listing after adoption". Total revenue was $251.0m, up 13%.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (transcript)
entries.mechanism: Two distinct paths. Consumer side: Guru is a natural-language shopping layer that lets buyers describe a use case rather than filter a taxonomy, converting browsing into dealer leads. Dealer side: PriceVantage uses demand signal to tell a dealer where market demand for specific vehicles sits, and VINMax decides which listings to promote. Dealers pay a subscription, so the revenue path runs lead volume -> perceived value -> higher average revenue per subscribing dealer (QARSD), not through a transaction take rate.
entries.shape_justification: Every disclosed number is an input metric - leads, vehicle detail page views, days-to-sale, bookings - so S1 by test. Revenue conversion was disclosed only obliquely and never in dollars: the Q2 2026 earnings presentation states new product adoption was the largest driver of sequential QARSD increases for a third consecutive quarter, and total revenue grew 13%, but no AI-attributed revenue figure was given and full-year growth guidance was left unchanged at 10-13%. Treated as main log on the precedent already set by Cars.com and Zillow in this log; the marketplace-vs-tech-platform boundary is genuinely arguable here. Note the 60% and 50% figures are sequential, not year-over-year - a favourable framing that flatters small bases.
entries.falsifier: QARSD growth decelerates in Q3/Q4 2026 while Guru and PriceVantage adoption keeps climbing - lead volume rising without dealer revenue per dealer following means the AI produced traffic, not willingness to pay. Also watch for the sequential framing quietly disappearing once year-over-year comparisons become available.
entries.confidence_why: Figures verified verbatim in a fetched Tier A transcript, but they are vendor-side engagement metrics on the company's own products with no dollar attribution and a sequential denominator.

entries.claim: In its Q2 2026 results release (23 Jul 2026) CEO Sam Sidhu said the bank "also saw positive revenue impact, with select verticals delivering over 100% improvement in prospecting success rates as AI enhanced our ability to identify and pursue the highest-quality opportunities", and disclosed a completed pilot of an AI-powered loan closing process that closed selected commercial loans "in seven days, down from 30 to 60 days typically".
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings release (Form 8-K exhibit 99.1)
entries.mechanism: Two distinct revenue-producing processes. (1) Commercial prospecting: AI ranks and targets prospects inside named verticals, raising the share of pursued opportunities that convert to a mandate - a hit-rate effect, not a volume effect. (2) Commercial loan closing: an AI-assisted documentation and closing workflow compresses time-to-close from 30-60 days to 7 in pilot, which frees origination capacity and shortens the interval between commitment and interest-earning asset.
entries.shape_justification: S1, not S2. Both disclosed numbers are input metrics - a prospecting hit rate and a cycle time - and neither is a revenue figure. The revenue conversion is exactly the interesting absence: Sidhu explicitly asserts "positive revenue impact" and then puts no dollar, no basis-point spread and no loan-growth decomposition next to it, in a quarter where loans grew 16.9% and deposits 14.5% for reasons the release attributes to franchise build-out generally. A CEO who is willing to say the words "positive revenue impact" in a Tier A filing and unwilling to size them is the standing pattern of this log, stated unusually plainly.
entries.falsifier: Q3 or Q4 2026 disclosure that drops the prospecting hit-rate metric entirely, or repeats it without ever converting "positive revenue impact" into a dollar or a loan-growth attribution; equally, the seven-day closing pilot failing to appear as a production process with a volume attached. If the 100% figure is never restated on a defined base, treat it as narrative.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A filing, named CEO, specific figures - but "over 100%" sits on an undisclosed base inside unnamed "select verticals", the closing figure is a pilot, and no revenue dollars accompany either.

entries.claim: BHP's FY26 results (17 Aug 2026) disclose US$470 million of EBITDA from technology initiatives in FY26 - US$330 million delivered in-year plus a US$140 million exit run-rate - against a target exit run-rate beyond US$650 million in FY27; on the call CEO Brandon Craig said that "by the end of 2026, technology initiatives were delivering incremental EBITDA at an annual run rate of almost $500 million". Autonomous haulage is now roughly 50% of the truck fleet.
entries.source_name: FY26 results presentation and FY26 earnings call, via Investing.com renderings (BHP's own PDFs returned HTTP 403 this run)
entries.mechanism: Named AI applications sit inside a wider technology programme: AI-led leaching optimisation at Escondida lifting copper recoveries, predictive and preventative maintenance powered by AI to cut unplanned downtime, autonomous haulage across about half the truck fleet, and pit-to-port supply-chain optimisation. The disclosed EBITDA is the programme's output, not any one of these.
entries.shape_justification: C4 - non-tech sector, non-engineering function - and a textbook instance of standing cost trap 3, composite value metrics. The number is attributed to "technology initiatives", not to AI; AI is named as a component and never sized, so no AI-attributed figure can be extracted. It is also not cleanly a cost saving: improved copper recoveries raise saleable output, which is a volume effect, so the composite mixes cost avoidance with production gain. Logged once, in the cost ledger, per the single-ledger rule; the revenue reading is noted here rather than double-logged. The two figures do not obviously reconcile - US$470m FY26 total versus a CEO run rate of "almost $500 million" - which is itself evidence the construct is loosely defined.
entries.falsifier: FY27 results that do not report against the >US$650m exit run-rate, or that restate the definition of technology EBITDA; and the continued absence of any AI-specific decomposition. If the programme figure keeps growing while BHP never says how much of it is AI, the metric is investor-relations arithmetic.
entries.confidence_why: Real number in a Tier A investor presentation, but read through a Tier C rendering because BHP's own PDFs 403'd this run, attributed to "technology" rather than AI, and internally inconsistent between slide and call.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 earnings call (19 Aug 2026) CMO Cara Sylvester said AI-powered Teacher and College Wish List recommendations and more personalized app content produced "total wish list creations up more than 50% to last year, items added to these lists more than doubling, and conversion across our key back-to-school pages up nearly 20%". Q2 digital comparable sales were +8.7% and total comps +3.8%, neither attributed to AI, and no incremental revenue dollars were sized.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call transcript, and Target Q2 2026 earnings highlights release
entries.mechanism: AI-generated wish-list recommendations for teacher and college registries plus personalised content on the app home screen, applied to back-to-school category pages. Separately CEO Michael Fiddelke said Target's "digital traffic sourced from external AI platforms is growing more than 3.5 times the industry as compared to a year ago" off partnerships with OpenAI and Google Gemini, and named Chandhu Nair as a new Chief AI Officer. CFO Jim Lee disclosed Roundel gross billings +nearly 20%, Target Plus marketplace GMV +more than 40% and Circle 360 membership revenue +over 40% - none of which Target attributed to AI.
entries.shape_justification: S1: the AI-attributed number is conversion, an input metric, not revenue. Revenue conversion is conspicuously absent rather than merely unstated - digital comps (+8.7%) and three separate high-growth non-merchandise lines were disclosed on the same call and none was tied to the AI capability. The conversion figure is scoped to "key back-to-school pages", a seasonal category subset, with no baseline conversion rate and no counterfactual for a quarter in which traffic rose 3.6% anyway.
entries.falsifier: Q3 or Q4 FY26 calls describing personalisation qualitatively with no repeat conversion figure, or the back-to-school conversion metric not being carried into holiday. Also: a Chief AI Officer appointed in August with no sized revenue contribution by the FY26 close.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A, on-the-record CMO quote with specific figures, but a seasonal category-page conversion rate with no baseline, no dollars and no counterfactual.

entries.claim: In its Q2 FY2026 results release (10 Aug 2026) Rakuten disclosed that "the advertising business achieved high growth with revenue reaching 65.6 billion yen, up 15.6% YoY, driven by AI-powered search and targeted banner advertising on Rakuten Ichiba and Rakuten Travel". Group revenue was 665.5bn yen (+11.6%) and non-GAAP operating income 42.0bn yen (+109.6%). No AI-specific share of the 15.6% was given.
entries.source_name: Rakuten Group Q2 FY2026 financial results highlights (company release)
entries.mechanism: AI applied to ad search relevance and banner targeting across the Ichiba marketplace and Rakuten Travel, with AI also generating ad creative and running screening and bidding across large campaign volumes. Trade coverage (MediaPost, 10 Aug) adds that Rakuten's conversational chatbot shortened time from item discovery to checkout and raised average order value on Ichiba, with no figure disclosed. The same release notes that "from Q1/26, a portion of AI-related development costs are allocated to each business" - the run-cost offset is being pushed into segment P&L.
entries.shape_justification: S2, and the losers are rival Japanese ad platforms and retail-media networks - these advertisers were already buying inventory somewhere. Fails S3 test (a): the counterfactual purchase clearly exists. Fails (c): search relevance ranking and automated bidding are not a capability that appeared in the last 24 months. The entry's real weakness is undecomposed attribution: the whole 15.6% is narrated as AI-driven with no split against Ichiba GMV growth or ad-load, and no counterfactual offered. Subject scope: Rakuten is an e-commerce, fintech and mobile conglomerate, not a software vendor, hyperscaler or AI-native, so main rather than appendix - the same treatment given to Booking and Expedia in this log.
entries.falsifier: Advertising revenue growth decelerating back toward Ichiba GMV growth in H2 FY2026 while the AI attribution language persists, or no AI-attributed ad revenue figure ever being separated from segment growth in a later quarter.
entries.confidence_why: Real dated segment revenue at a named company, but the AI causation is an undecomposed management assertion in a Tier B release with no counterfactual and no AI-specific dollar.

entries.claim: On the Q2 FY2027 call (20 Aug 2026) CEO John Furner said: "The number of customers using Sparky is up 70% from last year, and the customers and members who use Sparky for shopping spend 40% more per order than others who do not." The per-order differential is up from the 35% Walmart disclosed on the Q4 FY2026 call (19 Feb 2026). Global eCommerce grew 23% and global advertising 38% in the quarter; neither was attributed to AI and no incremental sales dollars were sized.
entries.source_name: Q2 FY2027 earnings call (transcript via Investing.com, cross-checked against the TradingKey transcript and PYMNTS coverage); prior 35% figure via Modern Retail coverage of the Q4 FY2026 call
entries.mechanism: Sparky, a conversational assistant inside the Walmart app, answers open-ended shopping intents (Furner's example: a weekly high-protein meal plan) and returns recipes, meal kits and a one-click basket of ingredients, plus recognition of items the shopper already bought. The revenue path is cross-category basket building - the assistant converts a single-item errand into a multi-category order.
entries.shape_justification: S1, not S2, and the distinction follows the Amazon precedent logged 2026-08-12: a cohort spend differential is an input/behavioural metric, not attributed incremental revenue. Nobody has established that the same shopper spends more because of Sparky; the disclosed statistic is equally consistent with high-frequency, high-basket shoppers being the ones who try an assistant first. Revenue conversion is conspicuously absent rather than merely unstated - Walmart sized eCommerce (+23%) and advertising (+38%) growth on the same call and attributed neither to AI. Note the convergence: Walmart's cohort statistic (40% more per order) is now numerically identical to Amazon's Alexa for Shopping figure from three weeks earlier. Two of the largest retailers on earth have settled on the same non-causal disclosure format.
entries.falsifier: If the differential is causal it should persist or widen as Sparky moves from early adopters to the median shopper; if it is selection, it must compress as penetration rises. Usage is already +70% y/y, so Q3/Q4 FY27 is the test. Treat as narrative if Walmart drops the per-order figure, replaces it with adoption-only metrics (users, questions answered), or never converts it into an incremental-sales dollar figure by the FY27 close.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A, named CEO, verbatim quote verified across two transcripts - high confidence it was said. Low confidence as evidence of incremental revenue: an uncontrolled cohort comparison with unaddressed selection bias and no dollars attached.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 call (19 Aug 2026) Lowe's disclosed that "customers who engage with Mylow while browsing online convert at three times the rate of those who don't", and that Mylow has fielded approximately 25 million customer and associate questions since launch. No revenue, basket or ticket figure was attributed to Mylow, and the quarter's positive comparable sales were not attributed to AI.
entries.source_name: Q2 2026 earnings call (full transcript via Benzinga; figure cross-checked against Retail TouchPoints coverage of the same call)
entries.mechanism: Mylow is a generative assistant on lowes.com answering home-improvement project questions in session; the same engine powers a Mylow Companion application for store associates. The claimed revenue path is intent resolution - a shopper who gets a project question answered mid-session completes the purchase instead of abandoning.
entries.shape_justification: S1: conversion rate is an input metric, not revenue. Revenue conversion conspicuously absent - Lowe's put no dollars, ticket or basket figure against Mylow on the same call where it reported comps and raised its store target. Selection bias is severe and unaddressed in the specific direction that inflates the number: a shopper who stops to ask a project question is deeper in purchase intent than the average browser, so a 3x conversion gap is the expected result even if Mylow were inert. Not S2 because no incremental revenue is attributed; not S3 because these buyers were already buying home-improvement product from Lowe's or a competitor.
entries.falsifier: A 3x gap should compress toward 1x as Mylow reaches the median shopper rather than the self-selected early cohort. Treat as narrative if Lowe's stops repeating the multiple, or if by FY27 it has still never converted it into a ticket, basket or digital-sales dollar figure. Direct comparator on the board: Home Depot ran the same play in the same week (Magic Apron, millions of questions per month) and disclosed no conversion figure at all.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call and the figure is confirmed in two independent renderings of the transcript. Low as ROI evidence: an uncontrolled cohort ratio with no baseline conversion rate, no denominator and no dollars.

entries.claim: In a Wall Street Journal interview published 17 Aug 2026, Albertsons SVP of Digital Shopping Experiences Jill Pavlovich said average order value rises 10% when customers use the company's conversational search and 26% when they use its more comprehensive assistants that match recipes and ingredients to dietary preferences. Follow-up on the entry logged 2026-07-26: the 10% figure is the same one CEO Susan Morris put on the record on 7 Jan 2026 and did NOT repeat on the 23 Jul Q1 FY2026 call. It has reappeared - in a press interview rather than an SEC-exposed venue - accompanied by a higher second figure.
entries.source_name: WSJ interview with Jill Pavlovich (17 Aug 2026), retrieved via PYMNTS and Supermarket News coverage; WSJ original not retrieved this run
entries.mechanism: Conversational search plus a fuller meal-planning assistant that resolves a dietary constraint into a recipe and then into an ingredient list. Pavlovich's stated mechanism is category breadth: "All of a sudden they're shopping across categories, across items, not spearfishing for that single item that they need".
entries.shape_justification: S1 by the same test applied to Amazon (2026-08-12) and Walmart today: an average-order-value differential between users and non-users is a cohort/behavioural input metric, not attributed incremental revenue. The 26% figure is the more interesting one and the weaker one - it describes the deepest-engagement cohort, which is also the most self-selected. What makes this entry worth logging is not the number but the venue. The claim vanished from the July earnings call and returned in a newspaper interview eight weeks later. Partial reverse-falsification of the 2026-07-26 entry, whose falsifier asked whether Albertsons would re-disclose a revenue-attributed AI metric at or above 10% - it has, but not where securities liability attaches.
entries.falsifier: The clean test is the Q2 FY2026 call (expected Oct 2026): does Morris put the 10% or 26% figure on an earnings call, or does it stay in press interviews? If AI revenue metrics only ever appear in trade and newspaper venues and never in the SEC-exposed one, that asymmetry is itself the finding and this entry should be re-read as evidence of disclosure arbitrage rather than of revenue.
entries.confidence_why: Named exec, on the record, two independent trade outlets carrying identical figures - but the WSJ primary was not retrieved this run, it is a cohort AOV differential with no dollars, no base and no control, and the venue carries no legal exposure.

entries.claim: Marketplace transaction data covering June 2025 - May 2026, reported by Fortune on 20 Aug 2026: AI-generated models are now roughly 1 in 6 newly uploaded assets on CGTrader but account for "$1 out of every $90 in generated revenue" (~1.1%) and 2.6% of sales. Only 5% of CGTrader customers who tried an AI-generated asset found it worked well, against 20% who found it inadequate. Alongside: Pew reports 52% of US adults are "more concerned than excited" about greater AI use, up from 38% in 2022.
entries.source_name: Fortune, reporting CGTrader marketplace data (June 2025 - May 2026) and Pew Research August 2026
entries.mechanism: Generative models collapsed the cost of producing a 3D asset, so supply expanded roughly six-fold as a share of new uploads. The S3 hypothesis this tests is the newly-economic one: if AI-collapsed production cost opens demand that previously could not be served, revenue share should track supply share. It does not - a ~17% share of new supply converts to ~1-3% of transactions.
entries.shape_justification: Counter-evidence tagged to S3, and specifically to test (d), newly economic. This is the cleanest natural experiment retrieved to date on whether an AI-driven cost collapse creates demand: the cost curve moved hard, supply followed, and buyers did not. It contradicts the standing assumption that cheaper production is sufficient for new TAM - on this marketplace it produced catalogue inflation, not a new market. Appendix scope because CGTrader is an online software marketplace and out of scope as a subject in the main revenue log; the finding is about buyer behaviour, not about CGTrader's own AI deployment. Two figures are given for the same phenomenon (1.1% of revenue, 2.6% of sales); read them as revenue share and unit share respectively - Fortune does not reconcile them and neither should this entry.
entries.falsifier: If AI-asset revenue share on CGTrader rises materially toward its supply share over the next two reporting periods, the discount is a quality-and-trust lag rather than a demand ceiling, and this entry becomes a snapshot of an early market rather than evidence against test (d). Also falsified if the gap is shown to be a ranking or labelling artefact of the marketplace itself rather than buyer preference.
entries.confidence_why: Real transaction data over a 12-month window from a named marketplace, which is far better than survey sentiment - but Tier C, single-outlet, self-reported by the marketplace, one narrow asset category, and the two revenue-share figures are not reconciled in the source.

entries.claim: On the Q2 2026 earnings call (14 Aug 2026) CEO Hermann Haraldsson said "only around 3% of our customers use our AI assistant so far", that those users "convert at roughly 2.5 times our normal rate" and "spend about 8% more per order". Separately he said that since launching AI model images in April Boozt has "produced around 10,000 of them", "adding roughly 300 new variants a day from just 16 reusable models", with "no casting cost at all". Group revenue rose 13% and EBIT margin nearly doubled; neither was attributed to AI.
entries.source_name: Boozt AB Q2 2026 earnings call transcript (Investing.com rendering), retrieved this run; adoption, conversion and order-value figures independently matched against GuruFocus call highlights
entries.mechanism: The same in-session assistant mechanism as Walmart's Sparky, Lowe's Mylow and Albertsons' Ask AI - but Boozt is the only retailer in the set to publish the denominator, and the denominator is the finding. At ~3% penetration a 2.5x conversion multiple and an 8% order-value gap cannot move a group revenue line that grew 13%. The AI model imagery is a separate, cost-side mechanism: synthetic on-model product photography replacing photo shoots, which is why no revenue attaches to it.
entries.shape_justification: S1: conversion rate and average order value are input metrics. This entry earns its place next to the four US retail cohort statistics logged today because it is the control on them. Revenue conversion here is not merely absent, it is arithmetically ruled out by the company's own adoption figure - and Haraldsson did not claim otherwise. Fails S3 on test (a): existing customers buying existing fashion inventory from the same retailer. The imagery disclosure is folded into this entry rather than opened as a separate C4 cost entry because Boozt gave a throughput number (10,000 images, ~300/day, 16 reusable models) and a qualitative 'no casting cost', not a cost figure - on its own it does not clear inclusion bar #2.
entries.falsifier: If the Q3 2026 report (late October) shows AI assistant adoption still around 3%, the 2.5x conversion multiple is a selection artifact of Boozt's most engaged customers rather than a lever. Confirmation would be adoption climbing into double digits with the conversion gap surviving the dilution.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A call, named CEO, and the rare disclosure of an adoption base - which is what makes the claim credible and simultaneously shows it is immaterial today.

entries.claim: On the H1 2026 results call (11 Aug 2026) CEO Elie Maalouf cited "the rollout of our AI-enhanced revenue management system, which has unlocked revenue uplift and market share gains for our owners." No magnitude was attached, and the H1 results announcement published the same day contains no mention of AI at all. Group RevPAR was +4.1% and operating profit +10% to $665m; neither was attributed to AI.
entries.source_name: H1 2026 results call transcript (11 Aug 2026); cross-checked against the IHG PLC half-year results announcement of the same date
entries.mechanism: An AI-enhanced revenue management system setting room rates across franchised and managed hotels. The uplift accrues to hotel owners as RevPAR and index gain; IHG monetises it indirectly through percentage-of-revenue fees.
