Separately in the half Maalouf said IHG "launched new AI-enabled natural language search capabilities within our award-winning mobile app and our website" and "launched an IHG plug-in within ChatGPT", both without any disclosed booking or conversion metric.
entries.shape_justification: S2 on the CEO's own wording. "Market share gains for our owners" is a RevPAR-index claim: the index is measured against a competitive set, so the gain is taken from the hotel across the road. Absent the system the guest still books a room somewhere, so the counterfactual purchase happens - fails S3 test (a). Fails test (c) as well: yield management by machine learning is a 1990s hospitality technology, not a capability that appeared in the last 24 months. Zero-sum at industry level and GDP-neutral.
entries.falsifier: A magnitude in any later disclosure - RevPAR index gain in basis points, incremental fee revenue, or attached System Fund economics. If the phrase recurs in FY26 results and through 2027 with no number ever attached, and never migrates into the written RNS where it would be legally exposed, this was investor-relations language rather than a measured result.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A venue and an explicit CEO claim of realized revenue impact, but zero magnitude and conspicuously absent from the written results announcement issued the same morning.

entries.company: Carnegie Mellon University / Larridin - 'Do AI Adoption Signals Predict Company Performance?' (564 companies, 538 after dedup, 478 10-K filings, 30,000+ job postings)
entries.claim: Cross-sectional study surfaced 17 Aug 2026 testing whether public AI-adoption signals - vendor tracker scores, AI hiring intensity, investment intensity and 10-K disclosure language - predict revenue growth, margin improvement or stock returns across 538 companies in 12 sectors. Only one signal survived: narrative concreteness, where firms at the top of the distribution are associated with 8.0 percentage points higher year-over-year revenue growth than those at the bottom (coefficient +0.080, p=0.009). Broader adoption measures weakened under multiple-testing correction, adoption showed little connection to margins, and no public AI signal predicted four-month forward stock returns. AI infrastructure suppliers beat sector- and size-matched peers by roughly 32 points over four months.
entries.source_name: CMU-Larridin working paper (PDF retrieved this run); interpretation via Help Net Security, 17 Aug 2026
entries.mechanism: No deployment mechanism - this is an attempt to price the deployment mechanism from the outside, using signals an investor can actually observe. That is what makes the null result load-bearing: if AI adoption were producing revenue at scale, the observable proxies for adoption should carry some of it.
entries.shape_justification: Filed against S2 because that is the shape it tests and fails to confirm - attributed incremental revenue on existing products at adopting firms. Counter-evidence, with one important qualification: the surviving coefficient is on how specifically a company *describes* its AI, not on how much AI it has. That is at least as consistent with reverse causality - firms already growing have concrete things to describe - as with AI causing growth, and the paper's own signals cannot separate the two. The infrastructure-supplier result is the picks-and-shovels finding restated: the measurable return sits with the sellers, not the deployers.
entries.falsifier: A later panel with the same construction in which adoption intensity, not disclosure concreteness, predicts forward revenue growth - or the concreteness coefficient surviving a design with firm fixed effects and lagged growth controls. Either would flip this from artifact to signal.
entries.confidence_why: Working paper, not peer-reviewed, and co-authored with Larridin - a vendor that sells the AI-adoption scores the paper evaluates, and whose commercial interest points at the one positive finding. The +0.080 / p=0.009 coefficient was verified in the retrieved PDF; the PDF's text layer was not machine-extractable this run, so the surrounding prose rests on the Help Net Security rendering.

entries.claim: On the H1 2026 results call (14 Aug 2026) CEO Amanda Blanc said: "U.K. Personal Lines is a great example. We have used AI in our pricing models to deliver over GBP 200 million of run rate benefits here. That is on top of GBP 100 million of claims cost savings previously mentioned." The GBP 200 million figure appears nowhere in the H1 2026 investor presentation, which quantifies AI only as accuracy and time-reduction metrics plus approximately GBP 40 million of claims cost reductions against a stated ambition of more than GBP 50 million.
entries.source_name: H1 2026 results call transcript (14 Aug 2026), cross-checked against the H1 2026 investor presentation summary
entries.mechanism: Machine-learned pricing models in UK personal motor and home: risk selection and demand-elastic rate-setting at the quote, so Aviva wins the risks it prices better than the market and declines or loads the ones it does not. Aviva has said it has used AI and machine learning in pricing "for over a decade," so this is an accumulated run-rate, not a frontier-model effect.
entries.shape_justification: S2, not S3. Test: absent the AI, would this buyer have bought similar cover from somebody? In the UK, motor insurance is compulsory and home insurance near-universal among mortgaged owners - every one of these policies would have been written by some carrier. Better pricing moves the policy from a competitor to Aviva and moves margin within the industry; it creates no new demand and no new insurable population. Zero-sum at industry level. Standing trap 3 applies with force: "run rate benefits" is a company-defined composite that Aviva does not decompose, and it is not a revenue number. The one thing that argues for the revenue ledger over the cost ledger is that Blanc explicitly separates it from the claims cost savings in the same sentence, which places it on the pricing and premium side of the P&L rather than the expense side. If a later disclosure shows the GBP 200 million is predominantly loss-ratio improvement, this entry belongs in C4 and should be moved.
entries.falsifier: A subsequent Aviva disclosure that decomposes the GBP 200 million into loss-ratio rather than premium or margin-on-new-business - or, more likely, the figure never appearing again in any Aviva document, having been said once on a call and never written down.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A venue and a named CEO, but an undecomposed "benefits" composite that is absent from the company's own written materials on the same day.

entries.claim: On the same H1 2026 call Blanc said AI has cut commercial-lines quote generation "from days to hours, which is driving higher conversion," and that in Protection "we have halved the amount of time it takes to review each case in medical underwriting with near perfect accuracy." The written presentation states the underwriting figure as "more than 45% reduction in case summarization time" at "99.99% accuracy." No bound premium, conversion rate or new-business figure is attached to either claim.
entries.source_name: H1 2026 results call transcript (14 Aug 2026) and H1 2026 investor presentation
entries.mechanism: Two separate revenue-producing processes. In commercial lines, automated submission ingestion and risk digitisation compress the broker quote turnaround, and in a broker-intermediated market the first acceptable quote back wins a disproportionate share. In Protection, an AI case summariser compresses medical underwriting review, shortening the gap between application and policy issue where applications lapse.
entries.shape_justification: S1: both disclosed numbers are input metrics - cycle time and accuracy - not revenue. Revenue conversion is conspicuously absent, and the absence is specific rather than general: Blanc asserts the quote-time compression is "driving higher conversion" and then gives no conversion figure, in the same speech in which she was willing to quantify a GBP 200 million pricing benefit. Aviva's H1 personal-lines premium growth of roughly 98% is the Direct Line acquisition, not AI, and the company does not claim otherwise. Note also the venue discrepancy on the same metric: "halved" spoken, "more than 45%" written, and "review" spoken versus "case summarization" written - the spoken version is both rounder and broader.
entries.falsifier: H1 2027 passing without a commercial-lines conversion or new-business-premium figure attached to quote speed, which would place this with the large majority of S1 disclosures in this log that were never converted into a revenue number.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A, quantified, and corroborated in the company's own written materials - but an input metric only, and the spoken and written versions of the same number do not match.

entries.claim: Aviva's H1 2026 investor presentation states claims cost reductions of approximately GBP 40 million, "approaching the greater than GBP 50 million ambition," alongside AI claims handlers covering more than 150,000 calls with more than 50% of personal-lines motor call routing automated, and an AI virtual assistant launching in 2026 to handle more than 15 million UK customer interactions annually. In Wealth, agentic AI automating quality assurance "will save 50% of time for our back office teams." On the same day's call the CEO referred instead to "GBP 100 million of claims cost savings previously mentioned."
entries.source_name: H1 2026 investor presentation and results call, 14 Aug 2026
entries.mechanism: Claims: automated first-notification-of-loss triage, voice routing and settlement decisioning in UK personal motor. Wealth: agentic quality assurance replacing manual file review in the back office. Non-tech company, non-engineering function, so C4 - the cell that matters.
entries.shape_justification: C4. Two traps apply and both should be recorded. Trap 3, composite metric: "claims cost reductions" is undecomposed and could contain indemnity leakage, fraud detection and handling expense in unknown proportion. More seriously, the spoken and written figures do not agree - GBP 100 million on the call against approximately GBP 40 million against a greater-than-GBP-50-million ambition in the deck, published the same morning. They may cover different scopes or periods; Aviva does not say, and this entry does not assume they are the same number. Trap 5 also applies to the Wealth claim, which is future tense - a projected time saving, not a realized expense reduction, and time saved is not money saved unless headcount or contractor spend actually falls. Aviva discloses roughly GBP 450 million a year of business-as-usual change investment including AI and data, which is the run-cost offset (trap 6) and is not netted against any of these figures.
entries.falsifier: FY 2026 results reporting a UK claims cost line that does not fall by anything like GBP 40-100 million, or a repeat of the ambition without a realized figure - and separately, Aviva never reconciling the spoken GBP 100 million with the written GBP 40 million.
entries.confidence_why: Tier A on both sides, but the company published two materially different claims-savings figures on the same day and reconciled neither.

**Neptune Insurance** is the sharpest disclosure found today and it sat outside the schema. ## The signal: Albertsons

In January the CEO put a specific, checkable revenue-side number on the record — **Ask AI delivering a 10% basket-size lift**.

Six months later, on 23 July, the same CEO reaffirmed AI as foundational, laid out four enterprise AI priorities (**three of them cost-side**), guided `$1.9–2.0bn` of capex toward stores and AI — and gave **no AI-attributed revenue metric at all**. Digital sales grew 13%, unattributed.

> **Companies repeat numbers that are working.** The disclosure asymmetry — specific quantified cost and productivity metrics from BofA, specific quantified capex from Albertsons, and qualitative adjectives everywhere the revenue line should be — is the actual pattern across every non-tech Q2 print read today, and it is what this log exists to measure.

## The confound worth naming

The added **MIT FutureTech / CMU** 10-K adoption study reframes the empty positive column. Two-thirds of deeply integrated enterprise AI adoption sits in the technology sector; non-tech adoption is described as only *slowly accelerating*. This log excludes tech as subjects by design, so **it is sampling the thin end of the distribution**.

That is a real confound: an empty log is consistent both with *"AI does not yet produce measurable top-line revenue at incumbents"* and with *"incumbents have not yet deeply adopted it"* — and nothing found today distinguishes the two. The falsifier on that entry is written to force the distinction over the next two 10-K vintages.
